title: Indigenous Peoples’ Self-governance Rises to the Challenges of Today
content: Indigenous Peoples’ Self-governance Rises to the Challenges of Today tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 17:06 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe Despite centuries of colonial assimilationist policies, self-governance among Indigenous Peoples is a living history that continues to unfold. And while Indigenous Peoples around the world have diverse mechanisms for self-governance, they all share the fundamental principles of an inseparable link among community, culture, and territory, as well as a collective vision of life and the exercise of power. For many Peoples this does not begin with the law, but with memory, daily practice, and the continuity of their own ways of organizing life. Self-determination is not a permission granted by the State. It is the recognition of a collective right that existed long before it was codified. Autonomy is expressed through practices passed down from generation to generation—most often orally—where dialogue, reconciliation, and communal life are real ways of making and implementing decisions. To govern is to care for collective life, the relationship with the territory, community safety, and the exercise of power. Colonizer nation States attempted to erase Indigenous Peoples’ organizational structures in favor of a homogenized identity, language, and way of living. They did not succeed in complete erasure, however. In various communities across Abya Yala, the assembly remains the space where ideas circulate and decisions are made collectively. Within it, leaders are not chosen based on popularity or purchasing power, but on their track record of service to the community. Assuming a community position entails a permanent responsibility and the obligation to be accountable to the people. Likewise, in many Indigenous communities, models of self-governance include a Council of wise people or Elders, whose role is to guide and support younger generations. This role is not acquired solely by reaching a certain age. It is based on the community’s recognition, a proven track record of service, and a life experience. Political life among Indigenous Peoples cannot be understood in isolation from territory. The care of resources, community spaces, and sacred sites is part of the very logic of governance. Justice, too, is understood from a different perspective; it is grounded in dialogue, reconciliation, and reparations. These forms of conflict resolution stand in stark contrast to colonial imperialist models that are based on punishing individuals. The coexistence of Indigenous governance systems and State structures has not been easy. Indigenous Peoples continue to operate within legal and administrative frameworks that employ complex legal and technical language and are enforced in a non-Indigenous language. When self-governance is recognized, it is typically in a partial and conditional manner. Indigenous authorities can exercise specific functions, though always within structures they do not fully control. These spaces, while important, do not equate to full autonomy. When Indigenous Peoples receive resources allocated by the State to carry out their functions, it further exacerbates the unequal power dynamic by creating mechanisms of dependency. Aymara women leaving the House of Justice after a gathering of community authorities in Chiripaca, Bolivia. Photo by Elvia Rodríguez. For a long time, States used categories such as “customs and traditions,” “local customs,” and “local practices” to refer to systems of Indigenous self-governance, thereby simplifying and diminishing them. Naming is not a neutral act: to name is to decide what is validated and what is left out. In response, Indigenous Peoples have insisted on affirming their forms of organization as their own systems of government—not only to be recognized, but also to reclaim the place that historically has been denied to them within the State. Although recognition of Indigenous self-governance has been gaining ground, putting it into practice remains fraught with obstacles. Policies aimed at Indigenous Peoples continue to be designed from a welfare-oriented and paternalistic perspective, focused more on meeting quotas than on responding to their realities, needs, and unique forms of organization, and ignoring community dynamics. All too often, the demands of Indigenous Peoples are downplayed or distorted. The case of the Māori illustrates this clearly. Their proposals for co-governance, aimed at building shared decision-making, have been labeled by some as “Māori privilege” or “ethnic elitism,” highlighting how recognition becomes contentious when it involves redistributing power. Another challenge is the inclusion of women in local governance. Attempts to increase their participation often fail to account for the burdens they already bear. Women take on community roles while simultaneously shouldering household responsibilities, doubling or tripling their workloads. For this, they are often questioned or discredited, even subjected to violence, based on patriarchal arguments rooted in exclusion. State policies have exacerbated these inequalities by failing to address the barriers women face or provide real support, shifting more responsibilities onto them without changing the underlying conditions. At the same time, Indigenous territories face the growing pressures of mining, monoculture farming, water and land grabbing, real estate developments, and tourism, leading to intensified conflicts, dispossession, criminalization, and heightened risks for those community defenders. In this context, political participation within State institutions remains limited. Even where progress has been made, such as the parliamentary representation of Māori, a fundamental question remains: to what extent does presence in these spaces translate into real participation in decision-making? Simply being present does not guarantee having an impact. The distribution of public resources has also introduced new tensions within Indigenous communities. Access to funding through government programs can generate disputes over their administration and control. In some cases, it has fostered internal divisions and corruption, consequently weakening the community fabric and complicating self-governance processes. Continuity of Indigenous Self-Governance Indigenous self-governance is not a thing of the past. It can be seen in the daily lives of various Peoples, who, despite changes and external pressures, have managed to maintain and adapt their own forms of organization within contemporary States. For them, autonomy is not an abstract idea; it is a living practice, built day by day. In Mexico, this continuity is evident in numerous regions. Data from the Oaxaca State Electoral and Citizen Participation Institute shows that 417 of its 570 municipalities are governed by Indigenous regulatory systems. More than just a statistic, this reflects the persistence of communal forms of government that continue to organize political life according to Indigenous Peoples’ own principles. In the Ñuu Savi communities, for example, the assembly remains the space where ideas are exchanged, and decisions are made collectively. There, leaders are elected, paths forward are agreed upon, and forms of accountability are established. Those who assume office are appointed based on the experience they have accumulated within community life and on the service records they have built as community members. These positions are, for the most part, unpaid, reinforcing the idea that authority is a responsibility assumed for the benefit of the people. Communal property authorities, whether agrarian or territorial administrators, demonstrate how governance and territory are deeply intertwined, particularly in the stewardship and administration of collective resources. For the Sámi Peoples in northern Europe, institutions such as the Sámi parliaments established in Norway, Sweden, and Finland have successfully created spaces for representation and dialogue with the respective States from which they participate in decisions related to their rights, cultures, and territories. These mechanisms have enabled progress toward forms of intercultural governance that incorporate Indigenous perspectives into State structures that had historically excluded them. These advances, while largely positive, also have their limits. The existence of parliaments does not imply a full transfer of power, and fundamental decisions regarding legislation or territorial management remain concentrated in the hands of the States. Even so, the Sámi experience highlights the importance of building spaces for dialogue and addressing the consequences of historical assimilation policies through truth and reconciliation processes. The cases of the Ñuu Savi, Sámi, and Māori Peoples are not isolated experiences, and demonstrate forms of governance that have persisted through their ability to adapt. Their paths have also been marked by resistance, mobilizations, and, in some cases, armed struggles that have resulted in loss of life. Faced with exclusion and dispossession, these Peoples have chosen to raise their voices and defend their rights rather than disappear in silence. Fully recognizing Indigenous Peoples entails more than creating international mechanisms and amending local laws. It requires transforming the way we understand power, territory, and life in community. In doing so, it opens the possibility of building communities where difference is not a cause for exclusion, but the foundation for a shared future. Elvia Rodríguez (Ñ’a Ñuu Savi, Ñuu Yuku Tuyuja) Is Cultural Survival Community Media Assistant. title: Sudanese women preserve bridal henna tradition amid war and water crisis
content:
Sudan
Inside a beauty salon in northern Sudan, intricate crimson patterns are being painted onto a bride's hands — preserving a centuries-old tradition under growing threat.
Henna is deeply rooted in Sudanese culture, particularly in weddings, where elaborate designs symbolise joy, protection and marital union.
But three years of war, severe water shortages and a changing climate are putting pressure on the plant used to make the dye.
Omnia El Sayyed, Beauty Salon Owner: "Sudanese henna is a form of adornment and a global calling card for Sudanese women. It is a distinctive feature of their identity. It represents ancient customs and traditions inherited from our ancestors. It is a cultural staple and a symbol of womanhood."
Farmers say unreliable irrigation is making cultivation increasingly difficult.
Abdallah Mohammed, Henna Farmer: "Access to water is the biggest obstacle limiting our production and causing drought. Water arrives at long intervals and cuts off just when we need it most."
The war has also disrupted trade. Before the conflict, Sudan exported henna directly from Omdurman. Now, much of the produce is routed through Egypt.
Mohamed Ramadan, Henna Factory Owner: "Before the war, we used to export our produce from Omdurman to destinations all over the world. Since the war, our produce is exported via Egypt."
For Sudanese women, keeping the tradition alive has become a way of preserving cultural identity amid profound upheaval.

title: Richmond Night Market prepares for its grand finale
content:
When the Richmond Night Market’s neon lights turn off for the last time on Sunday, the Metro Vancouver community will say goodbye to one of the region’s most vibrant cultural gatherings after 26 years.
The event, which ran on weekends from April to September, was founded by entrepreneur Raymond Cheung in 2000 to bring public night-time culture inspired by Asian night markets to the B.C. suburb.
Mr. Cheung announced the market’s permanent closing last month. He said the market’s lease near Bridgeport station was ending, and that the potential cost of taking on a new, pricier lease wouldn’t make sense for the business.
The market originally opened at Continental Shopping Centre in Richmond. Over the years, it moved to bigger sites, evolving into what organizers claim is North America’s largest night market. It drew more than one million visitors, tourists and locals alike, each year. The market hosted upwards of 200 vendors selling food, clothing and more in brightly lit stalls.
Since relocating in 2012 to its current location near Bridgeport station, the market became a major cultural and economic anchor in the region.
With its lease expiring and no affordable new site to welcome the large event, the only course of action seemed to be to close the market. “It’s a very mixed feeling,” owner Mr. Cheung said.
“The sad part, of course, is this is the end of the chapter. I didn’t expect this to last forever,” he said. “… But this market is about bonding, it’s about community – that’s what it is.”
For families like the Purbas, who drove from nearby Delta for their fourth visit this season, the closure cuts deep. “We’re sad that it is closing, but it is the last weekend we can attend, so that’s why we’re here,” Gagandeep Purba said.
The market’s reputation is known across borders. Jesica Vinson travelled from Seattle with her family to catch the final season. “Is there any way to save it?” she asked.
Behind the food stalls, however, many long-term vendors were feeling at peace. At Po Wah Dim Sum, Christopher Yee helped his mother, Lai Wah, wrap up a legacy of more than two decades running the family business. “My mom has been doing it for 26 years and she’s retiring this year,” Mr. Yee said.
Others, such as Francis Dela Chica of Bao Buns, have accepted the closing as bittersweet. He said that while it’s sad that the night market is ending, it was also the perfect incubator for small businesses like his own. “It was a good place to start, to test your products, to meet new customers.”

title: Pan dulce y manufactura son Patrimonio Cultural Inmaterial de la CDMX
content:
Aquí surgieron nuevas técnicas para piezas únicas
Conchas, chilindrinas, cuernos, gusanos, besos, orejas y puerquitos, parte de saberes y prácticas culinarias
Sábado 12 de septiembre de 2026, p. 26
El pan dulce mexicano, al igual que las prácticas y saberes para su elaboración, son Patrimonio Cultural Inmaterial de la Ciudad de México, al reconocerse sus valores culturales y sociales.
El decreto de la jefa de Gobierno, Clara Brugada, publicado ayer en la Gaceta Oficial, señala que si bien la forma de manufacturar el alimento fue introducida por los españoles, las necesidades y recursos propios de la panadería tradicional en la ciudad dieron lugar a nuevas técnicas y a un sistema cultural particular.
El decreto señala que la introducción del cultivo de trigo gestó una forma de elaborar el pan a partir de saberes particulares y generó, al mismo tiempo, un sistema gremial independiente, debidamente constituido y regulado, al trascender la actividad comercial en la que los panaderos comparten un sentido de identidad.
“Existen fuentes documentales que corroboran la presencia de panaderías y reposterías bien establecidas en la actual Ciudad de México desde el periodo de la Segunda Intervención Francesa.”
Enorme variedad para un sabor único
El texto que acompaña la resolución resalta que “el uso del pan en diversos actos sociales, tanto rituales como seculares, lo ha convertido en un elemento inherente a éstos, lo que ha dado lugar a la creación de piezas específicas para ciertas festividades”, y alude a un amplio abanico de piezas únicas por sus sabores, colores y texturas, que en panaderías llevan nombres como las tradicionales conchas de vainilla y chocolate, la chilindrina, gusano de canela, beso, chirimoya, cuerno, peineta, banderilla, puerquito, cocol, oreja, ojo de buey, mantecado, coyota o empanada rellena, entre otros.
“Se declara Patrimonio Cultural Inmaterial de la Ciudad de México a los saberes y prácticas del pan dulce tradicional” por constituir una manifestación de la memoria colectiva, las tradiciones, las costumbres y las celebraciones familiares y comunitarias, así como de los conocimientos transmitidos de generación en generación por la comunidad panadera”, señala el decreto que entra en vigor este 12 de septiembre.
La medida tiene la finalidad de salvaguardar los saberes y prácticas del pan dulce tradicional como símbolo cultural y social, mediante el reconocimiento, la dignificación, la promoción y la difusión de dichos valores.
De esa manera, dispone que la Secretaría de Cultura emita un plan de salvaguarda con el propósito de asegurar la identificación y divulgación de la expresión cultural protegida, incorporar la declaratoria a la Plataforma Digital del Patrimonio Cultural, Natural y Biocultural de la Ciudad de México.

title: Newman Rodeo's return for first time since 2019 draws 'royalty'
content:
Return of Newman Rodeo draws 'royalty' and riders from far and wide
In short:
The small mining town of Newman has been buzzing in the lead-up to its first rodeo in seven years.
The full-points rodeo drew competitors from across the state, including rodeo royalty.
What's next?
Event organisers and locals hope the event will become a mainstay on the town's calendar.
Rodeo royalty Ariana Rhodes is among the dozens of competitors who travelled from far and wide to compete in Newman's revitalised rodeo.
Eleven-year-old Ariana and her eight-year-old cousin Svetalina Stones trotted their horses around the red dirt arena that reflects the Pilbara town's mining roots.
The pair appeared at home despite it being somewhat different to where they normally ride in Lake Clifton, south of Perth, 1,200 kilometres away.
Newman, deep in the heartland of iron ore country, has not had a rodeo since 2019.
Royalty at the red dirt rodeo
Crowned Rodeo Mini Princess last year, this is Ariana's first Newman Rodeo.
"I'm competing in barrel racing and pole bending," she said.
"My favourite's barrel racing."
Svetalina hopes to follow in her older cousin's footsteps and did not hesitate when asked about her favourite event.
"Barrel racing," she said with conviction.
Newman was the furthest she had travelled for rodeo.
The royal family lived up to their title, taking out medals for their events.
Ariana placed first in her class for barrel racing and pole bending, while Svetalina placed third in barrel racing and second in pole bending.
Talk of the town
Locals warmly welcomed the rodeo's return.
Shire of East Pilbara president Anthony Middleton said Newman had been quietly buzzing in the lead-up to the event.
"There's a fair bit of talk; it hasn't happened since before COVID," he said.
"I didn't realise how important it was to the community … it's exciting to see."
Newman Campdraft and Rodeo Association president Cameron Wilson said it was special to bring rodeo back to Newman.
"It's going to be great for the town, great for the people, and just great to see it back in Newman," he said.
Mr Hall believed the turnout would be close to 1,300 people.
"I just think it's a great exercise for the town to show what we can produce; obviously, being such a small mining town, we don't have a lot of major events," he said.
"If we can establish this and keep it a recurring thing, I think it's only going to get bigger and better year on year."
Bringing rodeo back to the Pilbara
Launching Roebourne Rodeo last year, Karlayura Rodeo co-founder Tui Magner said it made sense for Karlayura to bring rodeo back to Newman.
"Myself, Brian Tucker and Georgina Bobby have really big dreams to activate rodeos more in the Pilbara," Ms Magner said.
"Doing Roebourne Rodeo in the west Pilbara, now coming over to the east has sort of been a perfect next step to build on that success.
"Newman itself has quite a long history in rodeo … we're just really trying to build on that success."
Competitors from as far north as the Kimberley region and as far away as the South West travelled for the full-points event.
Fellow Karlayura co-founder Georgina Bobby said Newman held a special place in the Karlayura team's heart.
"This place is in Nyiyiparli country, which is Brian Tucker's mother's homeland," she said.
"I think he wanted to bring it back here for his people."
Ms Bobby highlighted the relationship between Aboriginal stockmen and modern-day rodeo.
"Back in the day, the elders, old people then, they pretty much worked on stations," she said.
"It'll be good for them to see something that's come back with this rodeo, recognising those people."

title: The diamond jubilee of India’s green shield: Indian Forest Service completes 60 years
content:
The diamond jubilee of India’s green shield: Indian Forest Service completes 60 years
Corbett transitioned from a hunter of man-eaters to a wildlife champion, helping establish India's first National Park in 1936.
At the borders of Kuno National Park where India's famous Project Cheetah is underway, high-tech conservation meets human survival. Solar smart fences, thermal cameras, and satellites guard one side, while villages pressure nature on the other. This juxtaposition defines the frontline of the Indian Forest Service, which recently marked six decades since its modern inception on 1 July 1966.
The roots of the Service trace back to 1864, when Germany's Sir Dietrich Brandis became India's first Inspector General of Forests, replacing chaotic jungle exploitation with scientific forestry. Later, legendary figures like Jim Corbett gave the Service its soul, shifting forestry from timber production to habitat protection. Corbett transitioned from a hunter of man-eaters to a wildlife champion, helping establish India's first National Park in 1936. This trajectory led to the 1966 constitutional formalisation of the modern Indian Forest Service as an elite All India Service (AIS) dedicated to ecological governance, mitigating climate change, and halting habitat loss.
Also Read | Posting IFS officers as rural development project directors will paralyse public services: PMK
Global Standing and Mindset Shift
India holds 2.2% of global land while supporting 18% of the human population and heavy livestock pressures. Despite this, structured conservation has placed India among the world's top ten forest-rich nations. According to the FAO’s Global Forest Resource Assessment, India ranks 9th globally in total forest area and 3rd for net annual forest cover gains, with its canopy covering 25.17% of the landmass.This expanding canopy supports India's target of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2070. To meet this, the nation plans to sequester an additional 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes (GT) of CO2 equivalents through enhanced green cover by 2030. Alongside carbon sink expansion, India has rapidly expanded its network of Ramsar sites, vastly upgrading vital wetland protections.
This growth required a major policy shift. While the 1952 National Forest Policy treated woods as commercial assets, the 1988 policy subordinated industrial profits to ecological balance. This shift birthed Joint Forest Management (JFM) in 1990, giving communities a share of forest benefits and steadily replacing the traditional paradigm of bitter human-wildlife conflict with a sustainable ethos of human-wildlife coexistence.Legal and Modern PillarsThe green governance relies on a powerful legal architecture anchored by the historical Indian Forest Act (IFA) of 1927, which provides vital enforcement teeth for field staff.
Over decades, it has transitioned to work alongside a modern quartet of laws evolved by the Service: the Wildlife Protection Act, the Forest Conservation Act (FCA) 1980—renamed the Van Sanrakshan evam Samwardhan Adhiniyam in 2023—the Biological Diversity Act, and the Forest Rights Act (FRA). The 1980 legislation sharply reduced unchecked wilderness conversion. Today, developers pay the net present value of diversions into the CAMPA fund for large-scale afforestation.
Legal protection strengthened further with the landmark T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad (1996) case, where the Supreme Court expanded jurisdiction to all lands matching the dictionary definition of a "forest," making the Service the sole custodian of green cover. Down at the community level, the FRA of 2006 recognized traditional dwellers' rights, reducing distress migration and securing local livelihoods.
On the ground, the National Working Plan Code has evolved from counting logs into a scientific blueprint tracking carbon capture and watershed health. Young officers entering the Indira Gandhi National Forest Academy (IGNFA) frequently hold advanced degrees in engineering, medicine, and data analytics. They oversee a frontline equipped with the M-STrIPES platform, a digital net connecting handheld patrol modules with a central GIS analytical engine. This accountability has scaled up Project Tiger (58 Tiger Reserves) and Project Elephant (33 Reserves), helping India host an estimated 3,682 wild tigers and 22,446 wild elephants.
Also Read | Ecological equity needs constitutional protection
The Frontline Reality
However, technology cannot execute an arrest. Humans must still march into pitch-black jungles to face armed timber syndicates, poachers, and sand mafias. This danger continues to extract a heavy cost; over sixty years, hundreds of forest personnel, including officers, have died in the line of duty. The Service honours the historic martyrdom of heroes like Kirti Chakra P. Srinivas, killed by the smuggler Veerappan, and Sanjay Singh, who made the supreme sacrifice fighting mining mafias.
Today's green guards also face climate-driven forest fires, urbanization challenges, and invasive weeds choking grasslands. Yet, by leveraging smart technologies and local partnerships, the frontline continues to actively foster human-wildlife coexistence in rapidly changing landscapes. Inspiringly, this frontline is getting increasingly inclusive, with women making up nearly 20 percent of the incoming batches of officer trainees. The journey of the Service proves a determined nation can prioritize growth without compromising on its wilderness.
As the renowned author Ruskin Bond told Indian Foresters:
"Without your help to Nature's thrust,
This land would be a bowl of dust."
Our future livability rests on the shoulders of these guards celebrating the completion of 60 years of the green frame. In ensuring that our forests breathe, they ensure that India thrives. Their silent sentinel remains the ultimate shield for our collective tomorrow.
(Raj Kumar Bajpai is an Additional Director with the Indian Forest Services 1994 Batch, Jharkhand Cadre).

title: For Des Marcus, Malaysia Day is about bringing communities together
content:
As the country celebrates Malaysia Day, the 36-year-old Bidayuh from Serian, Sarawak, believes that spirit of looking out for one another is an important part of what brings Malaysians together.
“I know what it feels like to go through difficult times and to have limited resources,” Des told FMT Lifestyle. “So, as I became more stable and capable of giving back, I felt that it was the right time for me to do something meaningful for others and for the community.”
He has put that belief into practice through two very different projects this year.
Born Desmond Anak Markus, Des is a corporate communication manager who also performs as a singer, model and host. Known for songs such as “Cinta Aku”, he was also first runner-up in Mr Native Borneo 2025.
The youngest of four siblings, he grew up in a family where finances were often tight. His mother worked in a factory, while his father was a lorry driver who passed away while Des was studying at university.
Those experiences have stayed with him and continue to shape the way he sees people facing hardship.
His first initiative took place during Chinese New Year this year, when he helped organise an inclusive festive gathering for members of the visually impaired community.
The event was carried out with the support of an events company and the Mr & Miss Native Borneo organisation, with Des serving as organising chairman.
He said spending time with members of the visually impaired community reminded him that people experience life in different ways. It also broadened his understanding of what it means to support others.
“It’s not always about providing something material; sometimes being present, listening, spending time together and making someone feel included can be just as meaningful,” he said.
A few months later, he organised a beach-cleaning programme at Kampung Santubong with Sarawak Skills, focusing on environmental responsibility and encouraging people to care for the places around them.
Working alongside volunteers showed him the value of collective action and how seemingly small individual efforts can add up.
“Individually, picking up one piece of rubbish may seem like a very small action, but when many people do it together, the impact becomes visible,” he said.
Although one project focused on people and the other on the environment, Des sees both as rooted in the same values.
“For me, giving back is about sharing love, care and positive energy. I may have started with small initiatives, but I hope they can grow into something bigger.”
His outlook, he believes, is partly rooted in his Bidayuh upbringing. Growing up, Des was surrounded by values such as togetherness, cooperation and respect – lessons he now tries to carry beyond his own community.
He also hopes Malaysians will become more curious about the Bidayuh and discover the richness of their culture, language and traditions.
Music, he believes, is one of the most powerful and enjoyable ways to introduce that culture to a wider audience, and he hopes to do so through his upcoming projects.
This Malaysia Day, Des hopes more people will recognise that, despite differences in culture, background and experience, everyone has a part to play in building a stronger society.
“The beauty of Malaysia is that we do not all have to be the same in order to stand together. Our diversity is our identity, and our unity is our strength.
“At the end of the day, despite our differences, we all share the same home.”

title: Sustainability, Vol. 18, Pages 9102: African American Family Fishing as Food Provision, Communal Learning, Wellness, and Social-Sustainability Exploration
content: This narrative literature review examines African American family fishing as a historically grounded practice of food provision, cultural continuity, place-based learning, and environmental stewardship, and considers its conceptual relationship to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The review synthesizes an analytical corpus of 41 works spanning history, fishing participation, food insecurity, food sovereignty, foodways, place attachment, environmental education, and social-ecological systems. The literature indicates that Black fishing cannot be understood as recreation alone; historically and contemporarily, it has connected food acquisition, family interaction, livelihood, cultural memory, and community identity. These functions are conceptually aligned with SDGs 2, 3, and 10 through plausible pathways involving culturally meaningful food access, family-centered outdoor activity, and attention to racial disparities in food security, environmental access, and institutional representation. Family fishing may also provide a place-based learning context relevant to SDG 4, while responsible harvesting, reduced waste, and ecological literacy may contribute to SDG 12. Repeated engagement with local waters may cultivate belonging and stewardship; freshwater relationships are most directly relevant to SDG 6, whereas coastal, estuarine, and marine contexts may contribute to SDG 14. These are interpretive alignments, not measured SDG outcomes. The review concludes that family-centered pilot initiatives may productively integrate cultural history, ecological education, food skills, mentorship, and community leadership, subject to feasibility testing and empirical evaluation. Contemporary family-level research is needed to examine harvest, food sharing, learning, health, access, and stewardship across generations.

title: Más de cinco años para llevar su cultura a las aulas: “Me decían: no hables en tu idioma”
content:
Más de cinco años para llevar su cultura a las aulas: “Me decían: no hables en tu idioma”
Las nacionalidades amazónicas Siekopaai y A’i Cofán y Waorani lograron que el Ministerio de Educación de Ecuador reconozca sus tejidos curriculares e incorpore sus propios modelos de enseñanza, saberes ancestrales y lenguas en la educación pública
EL PAÍS ofrece en abierto la sección América Futura por su aporte informativo diario y global sobre desarrollo sostenible. Si quieres apoyar nuestro periodismo, suscríbete aquí.
Gaba Guiquita tuvo que aprender a hablar español a la fuerza. Sus primeras clases no fueron en su lengua materna: el wao terero. “Siempre hablaba en wao, pero algunos profesores me daban con la regla por hacerlo”, cuenta este waorani de 38 años. “Me decían: ‘No hables en wao’. Era un trauma para aprender español”, recuerda. Como Guiquita, generaciones de indígenas de las nacionalidades Siekopai y A’i Cofán y Waorani han crecido con una educación que no recogía su cultura. Ahora, después de una lucha de cinco años de trabajo, los niños y niñas de estas nacionalidades comenzaron este nuevo año escolar con clases en su idioma, materias que les cuentan sobre sus tradiciones, cosmovisión y el conocimiento de sus abuelos.
Más de un centenar de indígenas llegaron hace varios días a Quito desde la Amazonía y marcharon por una de las vías más transitadas de la ciudad. “¡Qué viva la educación propia!”, gritaban. Era un día de celebración. Bajo la consigna: ¡Sembramos saberes, cosechamos futuro! niños, niñas, maestros y padres, con sus vestimentas tradicionales, caminaron hasta el Ministerio de Educación de Ecuador, en un acto histórico. Ahora, por primera vez, cuentan con currículos educativos elaborados de forma autónoma desde las propias nacionalidades y reconocidos por el Estado. Una pancarta con el lema: “Educación propia para un futuro con identidad” encabezaba la marcha. En el Ministerio los esperaba el Secretario de Educación Intercultural Bilingüe para registrar oficialmente sus Proyectos Educativos Comunitarios (PEC) y permitir su implementación en las escuelas de estas nacionalidades.
En Ecuador, la Educación Intercultural Bilingüe se institucionalizó hace 38 años, cuando en 1988 se creó la Dirección Nacional de Educación Indígena Intercultural Bilingüe (DINEIB). Se logró desarrollar un currículum de acuerdo con las necesidades de los pueblos y nacionalidades indígenas. Aunque para ese momento fue un logro, gran parte de la estructura tenía un modelo que no respondía a las diferentes realidades lingüísticas y culturales de las 14 nacionalidades. “Era un documento traducido. Ahí hablaban del Inti Raymi [una ceremonia ancestral andina], que no tiene nada que ver con nuestra cosmogonía. Y los profesores no podían enseñar eso a cabalidad”, dice Wilmer Piaguage, dirigente de educación de los Siekopai. Muchos acababan la escuela sin conocer sobre su cultura ni su idioma. Ahora, los nuevos textos incluyen conocimientos que durante años quedaron relegados de las aulas.
Mireya Nenquimo, una de las profesoras de la nacionalidad waorani, viajó hasta Quito para la marcha. Llevaba una corona de plumas amarilla y pintura roja alrededor de sus ojos, tradicional de las mujeres de su nacionalidad. La maestra resalta que este es un gran paso y que las clases, que iniciaron este lunes, partirán de lo cotidiano. Los niños aprenderán a trabajar la chambira—una fibra tradicional extraída de hojas de palma—para hilar pulseras, hacer canastos y, para terminar el año, elaborar una hamaca. También aprenderán a identificar la madera para fabricar una lanza. El objetivo es que la educación salga del aula y aprendan en el territorio. Nenquimo cuenta que los miércoles, por ejemplo, la clase será de recorridos por la comunidad. Los niños tendrán que observar lo que encuentran en el camino, registrar las plantas medicinales y animales que reconocieron.
Pero el conocimiento ancestral va de la mano de un elemento clave: el idioma. Todos reconocen que jóvenes y niños han dejado de hablar su lengua materna. Ahora el reto de los maestros, como Nenquimo, será recuperar y fortalecer su idioma. “Ha sido necesario rescatar nuestra cultura e idioma. Hemos visto que la mayoría habla español y queremos que se rescate nuestro idioma y se sientan orgullosos”, dice Nenquimo. En su comunidad, las clases serán dictadas en wao terero los lunes, miércoles y viernes; mientras que los martes y jueves las impartirán en español.
Pero no serán las únicas habilidades que aprenderán y tampoco se busca que se aíslen del resto del mundo. Wilson Criollo, líder de la nacionalidad A’i Cofán, cuenta que la nueva malla también incorpora el conocimiento del “mundo occidental”. “Un niño tiene que tener su conocimiento ancestral, pero también conocer estas tecnologías del siglo XXI”, reflexiona. “Si no, ¿cómo podemos defender el territorio de las amenazas?”, se pregunta.
En el caso de los Siekopai, el nuevo currículum de estudios introduce los conocimientos que debe tener un siekopai. “Los estudiantes deben aprender los nueve mundos. Uno de ellos, el mundo del agua, donde hay seres espirituales”, explica. “Era algo que no nos enseñaban. Solo aprendíamos desde la visión de la iglesia y lo evolutivo”, agrega Piaguaje, quien ha trabajado durante tres años en la construcción del tejido curricular, sin contar los dos años que dedicó al diagnóstico de la educación en su nacionalidad.
Cinco años para aprender en su idioma
El proceso comenzó en 2019, cuando los waorani se preguntaron cómo continuar con la defensa de su territorio cuando los pikenani (abuelos y sabios de la comunidad) ya no estén. Las respuestas apuntaban al futuro de las nuevas generaciones y la educación que estaban recibiendo. En 2021 se sumaron los Sikopai y A’i Cofán, que comenzaron sus propios procesos de diagnóstico en sus territorios. Todos encontraron una preocupación común con la extinción de su cultura: la pérdida del idioma. “Los más pequeños conocían lo más mínimo. Incluso muchos jóvenes y niños no querían ni hablar el paikoka [el idioma de los siekopai], solo hablaban el castellano porque pensaban que se iban a burlar de ellos”, dice Wilmer Piaguaje.
Ese año se aprobó la primera propuesta para construir un modelo de educación propia. Para Gladys Vargas, lideresa A’i Cofán, crear el currículum desde cero significó preguntarse qué conocimiento debía llegar a las aulas. “Pensamos en qué temas poner, dónde están y cuáles son los nombres de los ríos, cómo es la cultura. Si se enseña eso, van a ir valorando el territorio”, cuenta.
La construcción del currículum educativo no quedó en manos de técnicos. Fue más allá: participaron abuelos, padres de familia, jóvenes y dirigentes que se reunieron para recordar sus conocimientos: desde las historias hasta sus técnicas de construcción de casas, cestos y comidas tradicionales. Pero, en 2024, las nacionalidades se encontraron con otro desafío: para que estos saberes pudieran impartirse en las escuelas públicas, necesitaban el reconocimiento del Estado.
Fue entonces cuando en 2025, las tres nacionalidades amazónicas terminaron sus Proyectos Educativos Comunitarios y las mallas curriculares. Y, este año, los entregaron al Ministerio de Educación para exigir su registro. Pasaron ocho meses de reuniones, viajes a Quito y cambios hasta conseguir que fueran aprobados e ingresados a las plataformas nacionales de evaluación. Ahora comienza un nuevo camino, el reto es poner en práctica todo el conocimiento dentro y fuera de sus comunidades.
Este logro tiene un significado especial para las nacionalidades indígenas del Ecuador. Cada una tiene sus propios saberes y formas de entender el mundo. Y, aunque todavía quedan otras nacionalidades por recorrer el proceso, este es un paso más para asegurar su existencia en el tiempo. Para Gaba Guiquita y una generación de indígenas, este cambio tiene un significado personal. Él, como otros indígenas de su generación, aprendió español a la fuerza, después de que le prohibieran hablar su idioma en la escuela. Ahora, los niños Siekopaai y A’i Cofán y Waorani podrán aprender en su lengua apenas entren al aula.

title: Environmental Justice Starts in City Hall
content:
‘Whose Movement Is It?‘, a series co-produced by NPQ and the Environmental Justice Oral History Project, is a call to action for those at the forefront of environmental justice decision-making, drawing on insights, hopes, and visions for the future from some of the foundational women organizers of the environmental justice movement.
The United States used to spend an average of about three billion dollars in weather disasters per year. Over the last five years, that average has climbed to 18 billion annually, with 28 billion in 2023 alone. Cities are at the forefront of the destruction, facing more environmental pressure than they’ve seen in the last 50 years. In the past year, floods have shut down subways and highways in New York, heat waves have overwhelmed power grids in Austin, and wildfires in Los Angeles have choked entire regions with smoke and heat; all issues that have significant implications for local infrastructure.
Environmental justice depends on shifting that power upstream by making community input part of decision-making, rather than asking them to react after the fact.
State and local governments account for roughly 75 percent of public infrastructure spending in the United States, and zoning authority largely rests with municipalities. Cities decide where housing is built, where industry operates, where waste facilities are placed, and which neighborhoods receive flood protection or transit expansion. With this in mind, and in the face of newer and harsher climate disasters, cities will increasingly need to use their authority to adapt to an ever-changing future of climate change, a responsibility that carries with it the weight of decades of infrastructural inequity. This also means cities will need to do a better job of centering community voices and input in their processes, from the start rather than as an afterthought or checkbox at the end of decision-making.
Where Climate-Preparedness, Community Input and Development Clash
The agencies responsible for decades of flood-vulnerable growth are now deciding how to protect against it. In Houston, the same planning commission that approved dense residential development in flood-prone corridors also oversees the city’s 2017 post-Hurricane Harvey resilience investments. The situations are similar in cities like Charleston, South Carolina—now tasked with implementing resilience strategies like the Dutch Dialogues Charleston as a citywide flood mitigation effort. New Orleans and other low-lying coastline parishes in Louisiana, once the trail of plantation slavery, are now serving as a pathway for climate disaster, and so many more. Localities are being forced to carry the responsibility of responding to growing environmental strain while building resilience to ever-worsening climate disasters while guiding economic and infrastructural growth. This dual responsibility can force cities to make high-stakes choices in the blink of an eye, a process that often contradicts the participatory planning needs of the communities they serve. When the focus is on expediency— how fast can debris be cleared, how quickly can funds be distributed, how quickly can new housing be built—the communities most affected by these quick choices are left out of the decision-making process.
And when community input is limited to late-stage hearings or short public comment periods, the direction has already been set. Environmental justice depends on shifting that power upstream by making community input part of decision-making, rather than asking them to react after the fact.
When the focus is on expediency—how fast can debris be cleared, how quickly can funds be distributed, how quickly can new housing be built—the communities most affected by these quick choices are left out of the decision-making process.
Historically, the benefits and burdens of economic growth have not been shared evenly; low-income communities and communities of color have faced and continue to face higher exposure to pollution, flooding, and industrial infrastructure, even as cities promote green futures. These decisions have intergenerational effects on air quality, housing stability, property values, and public health outcomes. This can be seen in the Snow Hill neighborhood in Roseboro, NC, where Sampson County’s 1,300-acre municipal solid waste facility, equivalent in size to 990 football fields, is the direct result of rushed and racialized planning. Snow Hill has campaigned for over 50 years against North Carolina’s largest landfill. Residents demanded the County Board of Commissioners address the asbestos and toxic sludge being dumped, reportedly causing shortness of breath and headaches, while water pollution has plummeted residents’ land values. However, the Board sidelined their concerns as they favored the economic benefits of the facility as a funder of local fire and ambulance services.
A very different part of the country, , experienced a very similar problem with missing community participation in what became one of the biggest water crises in the country. Without warning or consultation, and as a cost-cutting measure for the city, Flint residents saw a switch in their water source from Lake Huron to the more corrosive waters from the Flint River. What followed was the corrosion of pipes, seeping lead into drinking water, and resulting in years of poisoning thousands of already vulnerable people.

As federal funding becomes less consistent amid longstanding environmental harm and new climate threats, the clear path forward for municipal governments is to move from consultation to collaboration, shifting their priorities from developer-driven to community-driven. This is a practice that acknowledges that communities do, in fact, know what’s best for themselves; after all, it is the residents who know best where traffic and pollution are concentrated and where health burdens are the highest.
Municipal governments hold real power over how environmental risk and protection are distributed across neighborhoods, and right now that power matters more than it has in decades.
Self-Determination Across Cities
Across the country, cities like Baltimore are growing and redeveloping under banners such as sustainability and revitalization, doing so with a focus on co-creation and community-ownership. Organizations like Climate Mayors, C40 Cities, and ICLEI are re-committing their infrastructural and economic development towards a green future.
And community-based organizations are more than ready to take up the torch of facilitating those partnerships. In New York City, UPROSE Brooklyn has spent years building climate resilience plans in the Sunset Park neighborhood grounded in residents’ knowledge of the waterfront, the area’s industrial mix, and the community’s vulnerabilities. Those plans have shaped citywide climate policy from the ground up.
Another example we can look to is Minneapolis. The Green Zones program targeted North and South Minneapolis, the neighborhoods carrying the heaviest pollution burdens, and gave residents formal decision-making roles in setting priorities for tree canopy expansion, cleaner transit, and industrial pollution reduction. The city funded community liaisons, translated materials, and held meetings in neighborhood spaces rather than the city hall. And in Portland, OR, the city’s Environmental Justice Action Plan requires city bureaus to consult with frontline communities before finalizing environmental decisions, embedding community review directly into the bureaucratic timeline rather than appending it at the end. These partnerships work because they begin before decisions are made.
Municipal governments hold real power over how environmental risk and protection are distributed across neighborhoods, and right now that power matters more than it has in decades.
With the federal government pulling back from environmental enforcement and climate funding, cities are absorbing responsibilities that used to be shared. Community input must be built into the early design of zoning changes, redevelopment plans, and resilience strategies. Community input is not a procedural nicety; the communities most exposed to environmental harm are also the ones who understand it most intimately. Giving them real power in these decisions is not just the equitable choice. It is the smarter one.

title: Verhalen van Jip en Janneke komen in het Urks uit
content: De verhalen van Jip en Janneke worden in het Urks uitgebracht. Begin oktober verschijnt het boek met de titel Vor alteed maos (Voor altijd vrienden). Eerder verschenen de verhalen van Annie M.G. Schmidt al in het Twents en het Sallands. De Urker uitgave is daarmee de derde Nedersaksische editie. Met deze vertalingen willen de betrokken organisaties regionale talen onder jongeren levend houden. Mensen uit Urk Klaas Barends schreef één Jip en Janneke-verhaaltje in het Urks voor een bundel met Nedersaksische vertalingen. Het smaakte naar meer en al snel kwam hij op het idee voor een volledig Jip en Janneke-boek in het Urks. Barends zocht mensen om hem te helpen bij het vertalen. Het moesten mensen uit Urk worden die de doelgroep, kinderen uit Urk, goed begrijpen. Hij kreeg acht reacties op een oproep in de krant. "Het leuke aan de aanmeldingen was dat veel mensen in het onderwijs werkten", vertelt Barends aan Omroep Flevoland. Niet ieder woord De groep van negen Urkers boog zich over de vertalingen. Niet ieder woord kon direct vertaald worden. Als voorbeeld geeft Barends de heg waardoor Jip en Janneke in het begin van het boek kruipen. "Daar is niet een letterlijke Urker vertaling voor. Dan gingen we met elkaar in discussie over welk woord we daarvoor wel moesten gebruiken." Stichting Urker Taol heeft daarna alle verhalen nagekeken en zorgde ervoor dat er qua spelling één lijn in zat. De verhalen van Jip en Janneke stammen uit de jaren 50. Tegenwoordig zijn er opvoeders die kritisch zijn op de in hun ogen ouderwetse rolpatronen in de verhalen. Zo bekommert de moeder zich vaak om het huishouden en gaat de vader naar het werk. Aan de andere kant zijn er ook opvoeders die menen dat de Jip en Janneke-verhalen tijdloos zijn. De twee sluiten vriendschap, beleven avonturen en spelen zoals dat ook nu nog gebeurt. Niet alleen onder de mensen die met Jip en Janneke zijn opgegroeid is het boek populair. Ook mensen buiten Nederland bleken interesse te hebben. Voor hen verscheen er in 2008 een Engelse vertaling van het boek.

title: Helen Eno-Obareki: Carrying Her Mother’s Light Forward
content:
Latest Headlines
Helen Eno-Obareki: Carrying Her Mother’s Light Forward
Her life is defined by compassion, hard work, praising and worship God. Since her entrance into Akwa Government House, Helen Eno-Obareki who celebrated her birthday on Monday, continues to inspire and put smiles on faces many in the state. Writes Charles Ajunwa
August 24th came with warmth across Akwa Ibom State. The day was set aside to celebrate Lady Helen Eno-Obareki, the Coordinator of the Office of the First Lady of Akwa Ibom State.
For many people, it was more than a birthday. It was a moment to acknowledge a young woman who stepped into a very big role at a very difficult time, and who has been trying to keep her mother’s dream alive.
Governor Umo Eno was among the first to speak. As a father, his words were personal. He called her “my dear daughter” and said he was celebrating her on her birthday. He reminded people that since she took over as Coordinator of the Office of the First Lady, she has carried the work with grace, strength, and a deep sense of responsibility.
“As your father, I am immensely proud of you and the great work you are doing,” he said.
The governor explained why she was given the role. After the sad passing of his wife, Pastor Patience Umo Eno, on September 26, 2024, he said it was both proper and comforting to have their eldest daughter, who had worked closely with her mother from the beginning, continue the programmes of the office. He was clear that First Ladies are not appointed positions. “They come with the governor,” he said.
Appointing Helen as SSA and Coordinator was not about politics, he stressed, but about continuity and family.
What made the message heavier was the mention of GIFA. The Golden Initiative For All was the signature project of the late First Lady, Pastor Patience Umo Eno. It was very close to her heart.
Governor Eno said he was particularly proud of Helen’s commitment to keeping those ideals alive. Through her work, she has continued to push her mother’s vision of touching lives, supporting families, and showing compassion to the vulnerable and the neediest.
And the work is visible. At the first anniversary of GIFA held at Ibom Hall in Uyo, Helen pledged to sustain the legacies her mother left behind. She listed what the initiative had done in just one year: over 15,000 pupils received school supplies, residents of rural communities accessed free healthcare through the GIFA Wheels of Hope program, and more than 5,000 women were reached with economic empowerment. There is also the GIFA Adult Education Initiative, where men and women from all local government areas are learning to read, write their names, and handle basic daily information.
Governor Eno prayed for her as she marked her birthday. He asked God Almighty to continue to grant her wisdom, strength, and grace to serve. He also prayed for good health, happiness, and fulfilment in all she does. He ended simply: “Happy birthday, my dear daughter and Coordinator, Office of the First Lady!”
Others in government also joined in. Uduak Ekong, the Press Secretary to the First Lady, described August 24th as the day Akwa Ibom and humanity celebrate a divine gift. Ekong called Lady Helen a rare blend of uncommon grace, visionary leadership, and deep compassion. In his message, Ekong said she has turned compassion into action. She has touched countless lives, uplifted the vulnerable, and stood as a pillar of strength and inspiration.
Ekong noted that on this birthday in 2026, they were honouring her tireless dedication, her radiant heart, and the exceptional legacy she continues to build. Ekong’s prayer for her new age was for boundless joy, renewed strength, and greater grace as she continues to shine. He signed off with “Happy birthday Boss!”
From civil society, Joy Solomon, President of the Pure Wisdom Counselking Founfation, also sent birthday felicitations. She joined brothers and sisters in Akwa Ibom to wish “our Dear mother, Our Noble First Lady, Her Excellency Lady Helen Eno Obareki a happy birthday.”
Her prayer was that God’s presence would never depart from her and that her light would continue to shine bright. She thanked Helen for being a source of inspiration and a blessing to elderly women, youths, and the younger generation.
“I celebrate you today and always,” she wrote.
The reason these messages keep coming back to GIFA is because the initiative has become the centre of the office’s work. Helen herself chairs the GIFA Board of Trustees. The programme was designed to translate global goals for women and children into tangible local impact. Under the ARISE Agenda of Governor Eno, the office has focused on dismantling barriers against the girl child’s growth.
At events marking the 2025 International Day of the Girl Child in Uyo, Helen spoke about education and empowerment as investments with high returns. She said when a girl’s right to safety, education and health is compromised, it jeopardizes not only her future but the collective future of the state.
“Strategic investments in a girl’s dignity, her education, her empowerment will yield returns across health outcomes, economic growth and generational stability,” she told stakeholders.
GIFA’s work has also gone beyond schools. In February 2025, to mark the first anniversary of the initiative, Helen visited the Medium Security Custodial Centre in Uyo to donate essential items to inmates. Officers there thanked her, saying her presence and donation brought joy and comfort to the inmates and support to rehabilitation efforts. She told the officers that her visits would be more regular and urged them to keep to the mandate of rehabilitation and reformation.
This has been another focus. During the 2026 World Malaria Day activities in Uyo, she called for stronger collaboration to eliminate malaria, describing it as preventable and treatable. She said it breaks her heart to still hear statistics of women and children dying from malaria. She stressed that maternal and child health remains central to GIFA’s interventions, and future programs will continue to prioritize malaria prevention and broader healthcare.
She has also pushed for birth registration. At an empowerment programme for families with twins, triplets and quadruplets under GIFA’s Maternal and Child Healthcare theme, she told health workers and traditional birth attendants to sensitize mothers on registering their children.
She shared that when her staff gave her a list of 330 babies, insisting on birth certificates made that number reduce drastically. Care packages were also distributed to families to help with the burden of raising multiple children.
The United Nation has taken note too. During GIFA’s first-anniversary celebration, the UN Women Representative to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Mrs. Beatrice Eyong, commended the Coordinator of the Office of the First Lady, Mrs. Obareki, for holding the vision to sustain her late mother’s legacy. The governor himself was given the UN Women ‘He-for-She Ambassador’ title for promoting women’s inclusion in governance.
All of this explains why Governor Eno keeps returning to one point: this is about legacy. He said the administration is committed to prioritising GIFA and other support initiatives for women, the elderly, the vulnerable, and the less privileged. He described Helen’s qualifications as experience, exposure, education and access.
“This is not a political appointment, it is a natural one,” he said, and prayed she would have the wisdom to bring even more innovation to the office.
For Helen, the birthday was a quiet moment of gratitude. She responded to all the messages with a simple note: “Such timeless moments. God bless all of you for celebrating with me.”
That short reply captured a lot. In the last two years, she lost her mother, stepped into public office, and took on a statewide initiative that serves millions. People in Akwa Ibom have watched her go from being her mother’s closest assistant to leading programmes on education, health, economic empowerment, and social welfare.
What stands out in the tributes is not just the title “Coordinator” but the way people describe her work. Words like grace, compassion, strength, and vision come up again and again. The Press Secretary called her a pillar of strength. The Governor called her proud and responsible. A foundation leader called her a source of inspiration to women and young people.
The facts back that up. GIFA has supplied schools, funded women’s businesses, taken healthcare to villages, taught adults to read, supported families with multiple births, and reached inmates with donations. That is a lot for one office to carry, especially while still mourning.
As she steps into another year, the expectations are high. People want GIFA to grow. They want more girls in school, more women empowered, more children registered at birth, and more communities reached with health programmes. The governor’s prayer for wisdom, strength and grace reflects what many are thinking: this work is not easy, and it will take all of those things.

title: In Odisha, drum-making traditions echo the rhythms of farm life
content:
In Pahandi, a small village in Bijepur block of Odisha’s Bargarh district, the rhythm of a traditional baja or drum begins long before it reaches a festival ground. It begins with the earth.
Of the roughly 530 households in the village, most depend on agriculture, growing paddy, millets, green gram, ground nuts and other crops. But for eight households of the Chamar community, making traditional drums and other percussion instruments has supplemented their livelihoods for generations.
For Judhisthir Sagar, locally known as “Kutru”, the two occupations have always existed alongside each other. He inherited the craft of making baja from his ancestors, along with the practice of farming.
“Making drums and musical instruments is our identity,” said Sagar while tightening the strips of a newly made mrudanga, a two-headed percussion instrument widely used in traditional music. “We have been doing it for generations. It is our livelihood. We are proud to continue it.”
Apart from the mrudanga, other percussion instruments made in Pahandi include the godi mrudanga, udand khol, madol khol, dubi-tabla, pankuch, dhol and nisan. Each has a different shape and sound and a place in the cultural life of western Odisha.
From soil and hide to sound
The craft begins with the khol, the body of the instrument.
The soil used to prepare the khol is carefully chosen. According to craftsman Baisakhu Rana, red or black soil without stones or other impurities is preferred.
The other essential material is animal hide, usually from goats or cattle. The hides are sourced from various parts of Odisha and, at times, from outside the state.
The process brings together materials closely connected to rural life. Soil comes from the agricultural landscape, livestock provide an important raw material, and the knowledge of transforming these materials into instruments has passed from one generation to another.
Once the basic structure is ready, the drum is decorated.
Amitabh Naik, 40, has been making traditional baja for more than six years. He learnt the craft from his paternal uncle and uses Sambalpuri printed canvas, bamboo strips, coloured threads and soil to decorate the instruments.
“My uncle taught me this work,” he said. “I have been doing it for more than six years now. I enjoy making the instruments, especially when I see them being used in our festivals.”
The connection with Bargarh’s textile tradition is hard to miss. The district has a large community of handloom weavers. Sambalpuri textiles are among Odisha’s Geographical Indication-registered products.
In Pahandi, that textile aesthetic becomes part of a musical instrument. Here, agriculture, livestock, textile traditions and music meet in the making of a baja.
Depending on its type, an instrument can take three to five days to complete. Its price varies according to the quality of the hide, its sound and the intricacy of its decoration.
Sagar says instruments made in Pahandi have travelled to districts of Odisha and other parts of India. Some have even reached Australia and Singapore through word-of-mouth orders and references.
But the value of these instruments goes beyond the markets they reach.
Instruments with a place in village life
A baja acquires meaning when it is played.
The mrudanga, godi mrudanga and udand khol accompany kirtans and nama yajnas, devotional chanting of the names of god. The madol khol is used during Karamsani Puja at harvest time, while the dhol and nisan accompany the Dalkhai dance and festivals such as Sital Sasthi, at which the wedding of Shiva and Parvati is re-enacted; Nuakhai, which celebrates the harvest; and Durga Puja, which marks the victory of the goddess Durga over the demon Mahishasura.
These occasions are closely woven into the social and agricultural calendar of western Odisha.
Nuakhai, for instance, is associated with the new harvest and the sharing of newly harvested food. Music and rituals bring communities together during these occasions, making the instruments an important part of village life.
Bargarh has a rich folk music and dance tradition that includes Sambalpuri, Sanchar, Pala, Khanjani Bhajana, Dulduli, Karamsani and Danda Nrutya. The traditional percussion instruments made by artisans such as those in Pahandi provide the rhythm for many such performances.
From village workshops to distant stages
Naresh Bhoi, a young folk musician from Bargarh, is a member of the Kalagram Adi Dhun Group, which promotes Odisha’s traditional musical instruments through performances. The group was founded by Rabi Ratan Sahu, an artist from Padampur in Bargarh who promotes folk culture through music. Sahu has been a research fellow with the Ministry of Culture and a general council member of the Odisha Sangeet Academy.
The group has performed at Rabindra Mandap in Bhubaneswar and Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in New Delhi, as well as in Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh.
“Traditional instruments help carry the sound of western Odisha to audiences who may be unfamiliar with our folk traditions,” said Sahu. “A baja does not end its journey at the workshop. An artisan makes it, a performer brings it to life, and a festival gives it meaning.”
Keeping a tradition in motion
Traditional crafts face pressure from changing lifestyles, mass-produced alternatives and shifting market preferences. However, Pahandi’s drum makers continue to find work because their instruments remain part of rituals, festivals and performances.
Their knowledge is also sustained within families. Older artisans teach younger members, while performers continue to use the instruments in new settings.
The village remains rooted in agriculture. Its fields provide food and livelihoods, while its workshops sustain other form of rural knowledge. Soil, livestock, bamboo, textiles and inherited skills come together in objects that eventually become part of a festival, ritual or performance.
That makes Pahandi’s story larger than the survival of a traditional craft. It is a story of how different parts of rural life remain connected.

title: Colombia’s Indigenous guardians adapt as pressures mount on the ‘Heart of the World’
content:
- Indigenous Wiwa families in Colombia’s Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta are moving farther downslope in an effort to preserve community cohesion amid climate and security pressures.
- The mountain range’s Indigenous nations continue to hold to a “law of origin” that guides their path amid intensifying pressures from armed violence, resource extraction, and climate change.
- Wiwa leaders describe sacred sites, rivers and forests as “living curricula,” inseparable from cultural and ecological responsibilities.
- Recent protections have expanded the protected parts of the Sierra Nevada and prohibited new bids for mining and fossil fuel extraction.
RIOHACHA, Colombia — Amid the low slopes of a tropical dry forest, families from the Wiwa community of Gomke are building a new home.
Their ancestral settlement lies higher on a lush mountain in the town of Dibulla, overlooking the Caribbean coast in Colombia’s Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.
Across this region, many Indigenous communities have been forcibly displaced by climate-related disasters or uprooted by armed actors. Gomke’s move to lower terrain, however, is described by community representatives as voluntary: a collectively led adaptation strategy to protect social, educational and spiritual cohesion amid intensifying climate pressures and the presence of paramilitary groups.
They call their new settlement Shegunamke.
The Wiwa have also acquired other parcels of land elsewhere in the Sierra, including at higher elevations. “We have left [those] untouched so that rivers, springs and bodies of water do not die,” said Roberto Carlos Coronado Calvo, rector of Shenzhawimaku, the Wiwa educational institution that combines conventional learning with the community’s language, culture, knowledge systems and relationship to the territory.
“If we begin clearing and cutting into the páramo [ecosystem], how can we guarantee life for those living below?”
Across the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, known to its peoples as Gonawindúa, or the “Heart of the World,” the four Indigenous nations of Arhuaco, Kankuamo, Kogui and Wiwa are navigating deep changes driven by agro-industrial expansion, legal and illegal mining (driven by rising global gold prices), the return of paramilitary violence tied to the drug trade, and accelerating climate impacts within and around the Línea Negra, their ancestral network of sacred sites.
These changes are intensifying pressures on ancestral lands and pushing communities to abandon homes, territories, and cultural practices.
Amid all this, the communities can still fall back on the spiritual and political framework known as “the law of origin,” which defines the interdependence of Mother Earth and all forms of life. It offers a way to deal with these changes, resist the pressures, and hold on to fundamental truths about humanity’s relationship with nature, life, and existence.
Knowledge as inseparable from territory
Within this cosmovision, the Sierra is not property or a collection of exploitable resources; for the communities, it’s a single living organism encompassing forests, rivers, wildlife, sacred sites, and human communities.
The law of origin governs this fragile equilibrium. This ancestral code guides the four Indigenous nations of the Sierra in maintaining environmental and cosmic order. As the mountain’s traditional guardians, the four nations view commercial resource extraction as direct violence against Mother Earth.
Mineral and energy resources — gold, coal, oil, gas, salt — are understood as her vital organs; extracting them is thought to degrade the natural architecture sustaining life. Yet they continue to be extracted: data analyzed by the Interamerican Association for Environmental Defense (AIDA) show that at least 120 active mining titles and more than 90 pending applications overlap the Línea Negra.
For Luis Enrique Salcedo Zalabata, governor of the Arhuaco Cabildo of Magdalena and La Guajira, upholding ancestral responsibilities has grown increasingly difficult. When private developments, mining and armed conflict restrict access to sacred sites, and agro-industrial and climate pressures transform surrounding ecosystems, territorial knowledge risks disappearing with the elders who preserve it.
The human consequences became visible in Serankwa in March 2026, when armed clashes erupted over drug-trafficking routes. An explosive dropped from a drone seriously wounded a young Arhuaco man and injured several relatives, according to the victim’s family.
After the military secured the area, the family was evacuated to Santa Marta and dispersed to different medical centers, an Indigenous health care provider, and temporary shelters. That displacement separated them from their crops, sacred places, community authorities, and a territory understood not as property, but as a living body.
“To be a woman is to represent the territory,” said the family matriarch. “It is to represent Mother Earth. When a woman is harmed, it also means that the territory is being harmed.”
Displacements, such as those experienced by the people of Gomke and Serankwa, requires communities to rebuild daily relationships with new landscapes while maintaining their connections to high-mountain sacred sites where pagamentos rituals — offerings intended to preserve ecological and spiritual balance — are performed.
A spiritual resistance
The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta rises from the Caribbean shores to snow-capped alpine summits. Its complex ecosystems of peaks, rivers, forests, sacred sites, animals, and human communities form an interconnected living system. Damage to one part affects the whole, Indigenous authorities say.
Wiwa knowledge keeper Roberto Carlos Coronado Calvo is combining training under traditional elders with studies in traditional education and interculturality. He sees education as central to cultural continuity amid the changes affecting Indigenous lands and societies in the Sierra.
“It allows us to heal the memory,” Coronado said. “It allows us to heal the territory. It allows us to heal the places. And it allows us to heal the languages.”
The Línea Negra’s sacred sites, rivers, forests and winds form what Coronado calls “living curricula.” These places hold knowledge inseparable from the territory and carry practical responsibilities community leaders seek to maintain amid the rapid changes taking place around them.
“At my present level of learning, I hear when the trees or birds speak,” he said. “Birds speak like people. I listen when they tell me what is happening or what is going to happen. That is called listening.”
For Coronado, such listening is not only a spiritual practice but an action guide: it informs land-use decisions such as leaving acquired forest parcels intact to protect rivers and springs.
“Reciprocity. Care for the trees. Care for the waters. Care for Mother Earth,” Coronado said. “We must protect, conserve and nurture that whole system every day.”
Centuries of Indigenous stewardship have produced measurable territorial protections. In 2023, Colombia expanded Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Natural Park by 172,458 hectares (426,153 acres), to a total of 573,313 hectares (1.42 million acres).
Developed with the Consejo Territorial de Cabildos Indígenas de la Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, a collective of Indigenous assemblies, the measure recognizes ancestral governance as an effective conservation mechanism.
The park is home to a recorded 3,057 species of wildlife, including 49 threatened species and 126 plant species found nowhere else on Earth. Notable species include the critically endangered blue-billed curassow (Crax alberti), the Andean condor (Vultur gryphus) and the jaguar (Panthera onca). It also protects the headwaters of about 18 major rivers, supplying water to the departments of Magdalena, Cesar and La Guajira.
In 2026, Colombia designated 1.5 million hectares (3.7 million acres) of the Sierra Nevada as the Corazón del Mundo Renewable Natural Resources Reserve. Located within the broader ancestral territory structured by the Línea Negra, the reserve prohibits new applications for mining and fossil fuel extraction.
Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has pledged to expand fossil fuel production and mining and pursue a harder, more militarized strategy against armed groups. While the former plan goes against the worldview of the Sierra’s Indigenous communities, the latter has found some favor with groups struggling from heightened insecurity.
For Coronado, Indigenous ecological knowledge represents generations of systematic observation that must inform wider society. For that reason, he said, protecting the Sierra Nevada can’t be left to its Indigenous guardians alone.
“When we care for the Sierra Nevada, we care for life,” Coronado said. “It belongs to all humanity. Everyone. And we all have a commitment.”
