title: Redfern Reckoning: Lily Shearer on Subverting the Colonial Gaze for the Stage
content: Redfern Reckoning: Lily Shearer on Subverting the Colonial Gaze for the Stage Country Australia agnes Thu, 09/10/2026 - 09:27 Issues Languages and Cultures Program 5 Main Image By Cristina Verán The word Moogahlin, in the Yuin and Bundjalung languages, means “to play” or “to fool around”. This spirited term—and the living philosophy behind it—expands through the work of the renowned Moogahlin Performing Arts, one of the most vital and culturally grounding forces in contemporary Australian performance today. Indigenous theater veterans Lily Shearer (Murrawarri/Ngemba), Fred Copperwaite (Bunuba), and Dr. Liza-Mare Syron (Biripi) co-founded the company in the deeply entrenched Aboriginal community of Sydney’s Redfern district, deliberately rejecting the standard western structures and strictures of theater to instead honor millennia of First Nations storytelling. Over the past decade and a half, Moogahlin has evolved from a grassroots, artist-run setup into a major force on the international stage; one that maintains a deep commitment to the community from which it sprang. Through landmark productions like Jane Harrison’s “The Visitors”—a touring work that inverts the colonial gaze to depict the arrival of the British First Fleet through the eyes of the land’s Original Peoples—and flagship platforms like the Yellamundie Festival, the company continuously champions independent First Nations creators and reclaims historical narratives. Beyond decolonizing performance spaces and redefining what theater can be, Moogahlin broadens its mission to include environmental and cultural advocacy through its biennial Baiame's Ngunnhu Festival, held alongside the ancient Brewarrina Fish Traps. Cristina Verán spoke with Moogahlin Performing Arts Co-founder and Artistic Director Lily Shearer about the political and social histories that shape their work, and how Indigenous storytelling remains essential to the larger projects of community healing and cultural survival. Lily Shearer and Natano Fa'anana (Samoan), Moogahlin's Executive Producer, en route to pitch a new play at the 2025 ISPA Conference (International Society for the Performing Arts) in New York. Cristina Verán: Tell us a bit about the beginnings of Moogahlin Performing Arts and the community it calls home. Lily Shearer: We, the company’s co-founders, started talking about forming something like this back in November 2007, following the passing of Uncle Kevin Smith (Walbung-Murramarang), a deeply respected actor and Aboriginal activist from Redfern, in Sydney. He’d been trying to establish a local Indigenous theater company, and his family asked if we’d pick up the baton and build something proper and lasting for the community. We officially incorporated on May 19, 2009. CV: While it’s become known for performances that can be defined as “theater,” Moogahlin doesn’t refer to itself as a "theater company,” as such. Why is that? LS: That was dead intentional. Western concepts of theater want to put artists in this box, requiring script-bound works and proscenium arches, whereas our mob has been telling stories for tens of thousands of years, across interconnected forms that combine dance, music, visual art, oral yaans, and songlines. Written scripts, in the Western sense, are a form First Peoples here have only really been using for about 50 years. Naming ourselves Moogahlin Performing Arts meant no one could lock us into a single Western performance genre, leaving us free to tell stories our way. CV: What was it like during those early years in terms of size, scale, resources, and before Moogahlin had a permanent home? LS: We started out as a grassroots, purely artist-run setup, working on a project-by-project basis. Each of us, the founders, kept outside jobs to pay the bills and keep roofs over our heads. For years, our office consisted of a single black filing cabinet that held all our documentation, dragged from place to place, wherever I was working. Though we lacked a fixed venue, we had strong relationships with the local Redfern community. CV: What makes Redfern so significant, symbolically and historically? LS: It’s universally recognized as the "Blak Capital" of Australia as well as the geographic and political beating heart of the modern First Peoples movement—where everything from the Aboriginal Legal Services to Koori Radio to the original National Black Theatre were born. Back in the late 1960s and ‘70s, our Indigenous civil rights activists here were exchanging ideas directly with members of the Black Panther movement in the United States. The central block of the neighborhood—known simply as "The Block"—is Aboriginal-owned land handed over under the Gough Whitlam-led federal government in 1972 after community members squatted in tents, right there on country, to demand land rights. This history also ties directly to the closing down of state and church-run missions from the late 1930s to the late 1960s. [Note: In Australia, the terms Blak and Blakfullas are used to refer to Indigenous Australians, not to people of African descent.] CV: What were the social dynamics like at the time, in terms of where people came from and what they were facing? LS: Those missions I noted were run like reservations, or residential schools, with the aim of total control, strict assimilation, and the cultural erasure of our People. When they eventually shut down, generations of displaced mob—many of whom had been stripped from their families under the country’s shameful Stolen Generation policies—had nowhere to go. They started coming to Redfern and setting up camp on The Block because nearby factories offered manual-labor jobs to people who’d been trained on the missions. Sadly, by the early 2000s, the accumulation of intergenerational trauma, poverty, and forced displacement led to serious issues for many residents with drug misuse, domestic violence, alcoholism, and crime. It also became a highly policed neighborhood. CV: Did these folks come primarily from Indigenous communities around Sydney, or from further afield as well? LS: Our people came from all over the nation after the missions were closed. First Peoples from as far as the Northern Territory were taken to Milleewas Half-caste home, Mulgoa NSW, in Western Sydney. Our people on the Mission in my hometown of Brewarrina came from QLD, VIC, and communities close by, but it was a handful of those communities all mixed up on the Mission, so they didn’t speak the same language and have the same ceremonies, they didn’t even have the same diets. When the missions closed, they came to Redfern looking for work, as they were trained as domestic servants and/or laborers. However, most importantly, they came in search of their families, to find out where they belonged. I was involved in a door-to-door survey taken in Western Sydney during the 1990s. There were mobs representing 63 different First Nations tribes and/or language groups living in the Blacktown LGA. Most of our people living in Western Sydney were relocated from Redfern as they were redeveloping The Block. CV: What were you engaged in at that time, and how did it relate to the movements you’ve mentioned? LS: Between 2005 and 2007, while working in Redfern for a mainstream company, Performance Space, I got involved at the Redfern Community Centre (RCC), and I helped launch “Gathering Ground,” a Community Cultural Development project, alongside Pact Youth Theatre. I then became the Cultural Development Officer at RCC, and Frederick Copperwaite stepped in to direct “Gathering Ground” (2008, 2010), while I acted as cultural advisor, to ensure 100% Indigenous creative leadership. Our focus was telling authentic stories through our own lens, as well as using that storytelling to process intergenerational trauma—which we did while also bringing in over 3,000 audience members a night. CV: How did urban development pressures in Sydney begin to impact this community? LS: Gentrification was forced upon it by the state government’s Redfern Waterloo Authority. Homes on The Block were knocked down, and families who’d lived there were forcibly relocated, again. The Aboriginal Housing Company was staunch in holding onto The Block, and began fundraising and working with University of Sydney design students to reimagine its future. CV: The advent of new arts spaces, and arts programming in general, seems to too-often herald and further encourage more gentrification, serving its newly anointed beneficiaries rather than the People already living there in community. How has that played out in Redfern? LS: Well, when Carriageworks Performing Arts Centre opened down the road in 2007, community mistrust around it was huge. People reckoned it’d be yet another elitist venue—like, for example, the Sydney Opera House—that would basically lock locals out. It took years of deliberate, unrushed relationship-building to bridge the Centre’s divide between itself and the local Aboriginal community, ensuring the People would be empowered to tell their own stories through its space and resources. CV: How did Moogahlin transition into a fully funded resident company there? LS: The major shift came in 2014 when the CEO of Carriageworks formally invited us to apply for residency, despite our lack of capital at the time. This provided our first actual office space, and partnering with them on grant applications gave us the organizational weight needed for multi-year operational funding. We secured our first four-year grant from the Australia Council for the Arts (now Creative Australia) for 2017–2021, and are currently in our third consecutive cycle with them, through 2028, matched by multi-year operational funding from Arts New South Wales (now Create NSW) since 2021. That baseline financial stability allowed us to stop surviving hand-to-mouth on project grants and actually engage in long-term strategic planning. Scene from "The Visitors" at the Perelman Arts Center in New York City. Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: Now let’s get to “The Visitors,” which has been touring across Australia and internationally in the past couple of years—including here at New York’s prestigious Perelman Arts Center (PACNYC). Tell us how this work came to Moogahlin and what its mission has become now that it is part of it. LS: It was written by playwright Jane Harrison (Muruwari), the author of Stolen, who had pitched the script originally under the title “First Contact” at Moogahlin’s National flagship platform, Yellamundie Festival, in our inaugural year (2013). Following seven years of dramaturgical development and community consultation around it, to ensure authenticity, it premiered at Carriageworks (directed by Fred Copperwaite and produced by Liza-Mare Syron) during the 2020 Sydney Festival. In 2023, “The Visitors” was re-staged under the directorship, Wesley Enoch (Quandamooka) and in partnership with Sydney Theatre Company, premiering at Sydney Opera House as part of their 50th Anniversary program. The play employs a kind of symbolic inversion of all the histories Australians are taught in school that are, in fact, contrary to our own Indigenous stories. Those British colonizers who recorded meticulous entries in their logs about us had operated under the assumption that First Peoples would never read them. But Jane went and found these documents, including many wherein British officers described Aboriginal People as, for example, "brutes" with "narrow heads, stocky bodies, short limbs, fish-like lips, and protruding eyes." Non-Indigenous audiences are often shocked to learn that some offensive language used in the play is, in fact, quoted verbatim from the official British records. She wanted to invert that colonial gaze. Scene from "The Visitors" at the Perelman Arts Center in New York City. Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: What should we know about the historical event around which the story is centered? LS: Set in 1788, “The Visitors” depicts six senior [Aboriginal] Law Men & Women, and one new initiate, from surrounding clans, convening in council at what is now known as Sydney Cove to discuss what they saw making its way toward them on the horizon: the British fleet. They begin to debate, per their own diplomatic protocols, whether to welcome, ignore, or resist the newcomers. Events in the play [such as a public hanging witnessed offshore] are drawn directly from colonial logs now reinterpreted through an Indigenous lens. CV: How has Moogahlin managed to design and adapt the staging for “The Visitors,” thus enabling the play to travel beyond major mainstage theaters and work well in different and smaller spaces? LS: We created three distinct production models. Version A is our mainstage configuration, built for major venues like the Sydney Opera House or the Public Theater in New York, and featuring a massive sandstone set piece we’ve nicknamed “Bertha.” Version B is a much more compact, flexible touring setup for use in regional theaters across Australia. And Version C, still being developed, will be further stripped back, ideal for performances on missions, reservations, and in community halls. It requires just the seven actors in business suits around a boardroom table, under basic lighting. When we were in New York earlier this year, to perform this at the Perelman Arts Center (PACNYC) in Manhattan, the cast even considered taking this version to a rock in Central Park to perform it right there. Scene from "The Visitors" at the Perelman Arts Center in New York City. Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: How have Indigenous Australian audiences been responding to it? LS: Mainstage venues often feel alienating to our mob, due to historical barriers we’ve experienced from such spaces. But during our 2024 national tour, regional venues reported record attendance for local First Nations community members—some venues, in fact, saying it brought out the most Blackfullas they’d ever hosted! They come to “The Visitors” because we’ve built real relationships with local communities, presenting a powerful narrative that had never been presented on stage through an Indigenous lens before. CV: I understand that some conversations that came out of the 2010 National Indigenous Theatre Forum led to the launch of your flagship platform, Yellamundie Festival. LS: Between 2008 and 2010, Wesley Enoch (Quandamooka), now chairperson of Creative Australia, had been in discussions with federal Arts Minister Peter Garrett about allocating $2 million toward a new National Black Theatre for Australia. We argued that funds should go directly to artists, script development, and commissions—not more “bricks and mortar.” In response, Wesley and Lea-Anne Buckskin (Narungga, Kaurna, Wirangu, and Wotjobaluk) convened the inaugural National Indigenous Theatre Forum you mentioned, in Cairns, so that First Nations practitioners from across the country could gather to map out sector priorities. When the number one of these policies was identified by a vote: reviving the National Aboriginal Playwrights Conference (which had been defunct for 17 years due to both drops in funding and a generational gap in the sector), Wesley looked out at all the attendees and asked: “Who will take on the responsibility?” The room went dead silent, because no company had either spare cash or extra staff to offer. Liza-Mare Syron and I looked at each other, though, and thought, “OK, we will!”—and thus committed Moogahlin to leading it (despite having bugger-all in our bank account). Creative Australia then backed us with $50,000 in seed funding and paired us with producer Wendy Blacklock at Performing Lines to help build and strengthen our own producing capacity. Moogahlin Performing Arts co-founders Dr. Liza-Mare Syron, Frederick Copperwhite, and Lily Shearer. CV: How did that commitment lead to producing festivals as part of its work of decolonizing performance spaces, and how has Moogahlin’s vision evolved over time? LS: We launched Yellamundie Festival—from the Dharug word for "storyteller"—in 2013, as a biennial national showcase dedicated exclusively to independent First Nations artists (We do not accept proposals for this from established companies). From the 50 to 60 applications we receive from around the country each time, we select six works for intensive workshop development, and showcase the works to the public and sector over 3 nights and 2 days. Under Fred Copperwaite’s direction from 2013 to 2019, the festival focused on script-based plays. When I became Artistic Director in 2020, I expanded the format to include two play scripts, two dance/movement works, and two music/composition pieces, returning us to traditional storytelling methods that treated movement and composition as equal to texts. Across its seven editions so far, Yellamundie Festival has developed 51 original works—21 of which have gone on to full mainstage productions with major companies nationwide. Moogahlin itself also commits to fully producing at least one work from each cohort. CV: Please describe what the broader landscape of Indigenous theater in Australia, especially Indigenous-led theater companies, looks like today, and what particular challenges are still being faced. LS: The sector remains relatively tiny, with just three dedicated Black companies nationwide: Ilbijerri Theatre Company in Melbourne, Yirra Yaakin Theatre Company in Perth, and Moogahlin in Sydney (a fourth company, Kooemba Jdarra in Brisbane, closed around 2008 due to funding and operational pressures). We do have several specialized dance and physical theater organizations to add to the list, including Bangarra Dance Theatre, Marrugeku, and BlakDance. Recognizing also our only national First Peoples-led training institution, the National Aboriginal & Islander Skills Development Association (NAISDA) Dance College. As to the challenges, we as First Peoples entities have to respond to demands that mainstream organizations rarely face, with our teams constantly balancing creative development with support for community needs—including the ongoing work of reconnecting families split by the country’s Stolen Generations policies. We’re also navigating the dynamics around what’s being called a “lost generation”: people who’d previously hidden their Indigenous identity due to systemic racism and discrimination, but now, without having grown up in community, proudly claim this heritage. Cast and crew of "The Visitors." Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: How did the familial and perhaps generational experiences of yourself and your Moogahlin counterparts shape your respective interests in and commitment to reclaiming historical narratives? LS: My generation grew up under Australia’s assimilation policies. First Peoples here were not granted full voting rights until 1967, and our equal access to education was only mandated around 1972. I remember well that, as a student in the mid-1970s, in a Catholic secondary school run by Good Samaritan nuns, we were taught that Captain Cook "discovered" Australia (and therefore us). I dared to challenge my history teacher on this point, insisting that, according to my father and grandfather, that man didn't discover us—our people discovered him when he arrived on our shores. For this, the teacher called me a "brazen toad" and threw me out of her class—permanently. My co-founders, who are also Indigenous, had quite different upbringings. Meanwhile, Liza-Mare Syron grew up away from community in the Sydney suburb of Balmain, while Fred Copperwaite grew up on the other side of the country in Fremantle, near Perth, with his white father’s family. It was at age 30 that he was finally able to connect with his (maternal side) Aboriginal family. CV: Moogahlin now also produces another festival, which connects culturally centered storytelling with environmental advocacy. Tell us about this, especially the significance of the place for its setting. LS: Baiame Ngunnhu Festival, established in 2015, uses performance and community gathering to fight for environmental justice. It takes place along the Ba-Wun (Barwon) River in my home community of Brewarrina (in New South Wales). The site features our traditional Fish Traps—called Ngunnhu—which comprise an ancient stone-pen system and represent the oldest human-made structures on Earth, predating the Egyptian Pyramids and Stonehenge. Despite its immense historical significance, unfortunately, the Australian government provides bugger-all protection or funding compared to those places it sees as global heritage sites. CV: And for the record, what are the most pressing issues for this community right now? LS: The river system has been severely degraded by imported cattle breaking down its banks, invasive European carp displacing native fish, and introduced weeds choking the water channels. Most damaging of all are commercial cotton farms—many owned by foreign corporate interests in America and China—that extract massive volumes of water from our river network, on the driest inhabited continent on Earth. The core message at Baiame’s Ngunnhu Festival is straightforward: if the natural country provided by the Creator is unhealthy, the people who rely on that land cannot be healthy either. Thus, we are able to link our cultural survival directly to environmental survival and, ultimately, to the survival of all our First Nations Peoples. --Cristina Verán is an international Indigenous Peoples-focused researcher, educator, advocacy strategist, network weaver, curator, and mediamaker. She was a founding member of the United Nations Indigenous Media Network and the UN Indigenous Language Caucus. As Adjunct Faculty at New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts and Affiliate Faculty of the NYU Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, she brings emphasis to the global histories, expressions, and socio-political impacts of Indigenous contemporary visual and performing arts, design, tech, media, and popular culture(s). Cast members featured in these images from "The Visitors" America Season, at PAC NYC in New York, include: Najwa Adams-Ebel, Beau Dean, Riley Smith, Sean Dow, Kyle Morrison, Guy Simons, James Slee, and Zoe Walters. (Additional members feature in the Australian and New Zealand Season productions.)

title: A Christian pastor called Arapaho ceremonies ‘idol worship.’ Now the tribe wants her church gone
content:
Savannah Peters
Associated Press
ARAPAHOE, Wyo. — Every Sunday morning on the Wind River Reservation, congregants gather at Foundations for Nations Church to pray while protesters outside do the same.
The two rituals have unfolded in parallel since the Christian church’s pastor, Sarah Lucas, preached a sermon condemning Arapaho ceremonial ways.
The Northern Arapaho and Eastern Shoshone Tribes that share the reservation have made clear that Lucas is no longer welcome. Lucas, who is not Native American but owns the land under her church, says she isn’t going anywhere. The standoff tests the boundaries of religious freedom and the right of a tribal nation to govern according to its own values and protocols.
The conflict stems from a video that circulated in July as Arapaho people surfaced from their weeklong sundance ceremony. In it, Lucas called that cornerstone of Arapaho spiritual life “idol worship.”
“Jesus is the chain breaker. He is the only God that we should be praying to,” Lucas said.
Lucas says her words reflect her interpretation of the Bible and are constitutionally protected. Many Arapaho people say she took aim at something central to who they are, reopening wounds from a not-so-distant era of religious assimilation and abuse.
With the smell of coffee and sweetgrass swirling, regular Sunday demonstrators were recently joined by activists from the American Indian Movement and Arapaho Chairman Keenan Groesbeck as they marched past ranchland and scattered homes toward the church.
“We brought in our ceremonial elders. We heard them loud and clear,” said Groesbeck. “They don’t want them here no more.”
Lucas condemned the highest Arapaho ceremony
The sundance marks a time of connection, offering and collective renewal. As Arapaho people closed this year’s ceremony and welcomed a new year according to their traditions, Lucas and her smaller-than-usual congregation prayed for them.
“You have generations, centuries of people doing this offering, going in and making vows to change,” Lucas said. “Father God, we see no fruit.”
Many Arapahos were stunned to hear an outsider not only disparage the ceremony but talk about closely held details that aren’t meant to be discussed openly.
Big Wind Carpenter, who was among the protesters, said Lucas couldn’t have chosen a more painful target.
“There’s nothing I could say to make non-Arapahos understand,” Carpenter said.
Lucas said she regrets her sharp delivery captured in clips that went viral but not the message itself. Since founding her church nine years ago, she said she has had “hard conversations” urging Native congregants to renounce sundance, sweat lodges and burning cedar during prayer, traditions she equates to idolatry.
“The Bible makes it very clear to only worship one God,” Lucas said.
Some members of her mixed Native and white congregation were unaware of her stance. Lucas said Sunday turnout is down half from 150. Some weeks, the protest crowd has rivaled church attendance.
Arapaho congregant Tearany Black, who considers Lucas a stand-in parent, said she agrees Native Christians should turn away from ceremony but found the tone of the sermon racist.
“She cares for our people,” said Black. “I just don’t think she understands where we’re coming from.”
On Wind River, ceremony and Christianity coexist
DJ Gardner grew up praying in sweat lodges and reading the Bible. He joined Lucas’ congregation last year and didn’t anticipate being asked to choose.
“I thought they accepted us,” Gardner said. “In my view, why else would you be on a reservation?”
The 28-year-old, who has walked away from Foundations for Nations, associates Lucas’ rhetoric with assimilationist boarding schools like the one his grandfather survived.
In part to repair that dark history, the Episcopal and Catholic missions that have been active on Wind River since the late 1800s now embrace ceremonial practices.
“It’s an irony of colonialism, the degree to which Native people have remade Christianity according to their own values,” said Michael McNally, a professor of religious studies at Carleton College in Minnesota.
Lucas interprets the Bible differently.
“I don’t believe you can have mixture,” she said.
Foundations for Nations grew through community aid
Mary Rose Goggles was struggling with the costs of raising her grandchildren in 2017 when Lucas knocked on her door and warmly invited her to join her new church.
Goggles, who practices Arapaho ceremonial ways but dabbles in Christianity, liked the worship band and activities that kept her grandchildren busy. As Foundations for Nations grew, she visited its food bank, clothing giveaways and events like a fall harvest festival.
“It was good to see the kids enjoying themselves. It was good to see my relations getting help,” Goggles said.
Lucas built relationships on Wind River by filling gaps. Her church offers free after-school and summer day camps. Visiting missionaries fill tribal members’ gas tanks and replace their sagging roofs.
Foundations for Nations’ website solicits outside donations to “revive, raise up and restore” Wind River, listing grim statistics about addiction, sexual assault and unemployment. The Associated Press found those numbers were pulled from national studies not specific to the reservation or could not be traced to a verifiable source.
A page asking donors to “sponsor” a child in exchange for photos and letters was recently removed.
Goggles left Foundations for Nations several years ago after moving away but thought warmly of the church until seeing Lucas’ sermon, which she said left her “heartbroken.”
Jenea Mandan has cycled through feelings of anger and shame about sending her children to the church’s summer camp. An Arapaho traditionalist, Mandan had misgivings about the Christian program but needed childcare help.
“At that time I was a single mom, I was in a low-income situation,” Mandan said. “It feels like they took advantage of that.”
The church sits on private land. The tribe still wants it gone
Lucas believes God called her to Wind River. But she deliberately built her church on private property within the reservation’s boundaries rather than tribal land where, she said, the tribes would effectively be her landlords.
Foundations for Nations is located amid a patchwork of federal, tribal and private property — the legacy of 19th century federal policies designed to eliminate tribes by breaking up collective land bases.
“That era has cascading effects that are devastating for tribal sovereignty,” said Jessica Shoemaker, a professor at the University of Nebraska College of Law.
Shoemaker said tribes have broad civil authority over non-Natives on tribal land, including to banish them. But jurisdiction over private property within reservations is litigated case-by-case.
Lucas and her attorneys with the Liberty Counsel, a conservative Christian legal organization, assert that her ownership of the property shields her from banishment.
In July, the Arapaho and Shoshone councils passed ordinances requiring religious groups to seek their approval before operating on Wind River.
“That’s the law of the land on our reservation,” said Groesbeck.
That has forced Foundations for Nations to suspend youth programming since it is now prohibited from picking up and dropping off children on the reservation.
In an Aug. 31 memo, the Arapaho council acknowledged that “jurisdictional limits” likely prevent it from regulating church activity on private land. And any tribal court enforcement of those ordinances could face federal review, where there’s a high bar for proving non-Native conduct threatens tribal well-being.
Meanwhile, the 21,000 square-foot (1,950 square-meter), steel-sided building that houses Foundations for Nations’ sanctuary, community spaces and indoor playground has been unusually quiet. Construction on a neighboring youth center continues.
“God would not have us build this and provided all of it to empty it out,” Lucas said.
Gardner has returned to the Catholic church of his childhood, where Arapaho geometric motifs adorn the sanctuary and he is welcome to burn cedar.
He has been praying for guidance on forgiveness.
“In order for me to strive to be like Jesus, I would have to forgive,” Gardner said. “But there are some lines you just don’t cross.”
This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press.

title: Koroneihana 2026: Iwi vow to honour the legacy of loved ones lost
content:
Tears and tributes have flowed at this year's Koroneihana, as iwi from across the country have gathered at Tūrangawaewae to remember a generation of formidable leaders lost over the past year.
Among them, Tā Hirini Moko Mead, Tā Whatarangi Winiata and Te Kepa Takataka-o-Rangi Stirling - remembered for their enduring commitment to te ao Māori and the generations they inspired.
Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Ngā Tapuwae turned out in force to honour their koroua Te Kepa just weeks after his death.
Ngā Tapuwae chair Scott Gemmell who led the contingent said the dedication of Te Kepa and his wife Pani Takawhenua Waipapa Stirling was reflected in the students of the Kura who spoke the language and carried their culture with pride.
"Ka mea ana ia ko te reo Māori te waka wairua ki ō tātou mātua tīpuna. Nō reira, kōrero i tō tātou reo i ngā wā katoa, i ngā wāhi katoa."
"He believed our language was a spiritual vessel connecting us with our tūpuna. He was proud of his students, and he encouraged them to take pride in their culture. He spoke te reo Māori all the time no matter where he was."
Hundreds of leaders and loved ones have been acknowledged and Ngāti Awa representative Pouroto Ngaropo said the loss of so many leaders emphasised the urgency of preparing rangatahi to step into leadership roles.
"Kua tae mai te wā a te korero a Sonny Waru, a tōna wā ngā rangatira o te ao Māori, he rangatahi, he rangatahi, he rangatahi."
"The time Sonny Waru spoke of is near, the time will come when our youth, our young people, our children will have to lead us into the future."
Dr Wayne Ngata said the number of tangihanga he had attended this year was overwhelming - but the scale of loss became a stark reality when iwi came together in Ngaaruawaahia.
"Ko au nei, kua hōhā katoa au ki te haere ki te tangi tūpāpaku. Engari i tēnei rā, kua whakahuihui i ō tātou mate kia taea e tātou te tiro tōtika atu ki te ora."
"Personally, I'm weary from mourning the loss of so many lives, we will always honour them as we do today, but here we have come together to focus on a brighter future."
As the kōrero shifted from honouring those who had passed to focusing on those still here, the tone changed drastically.
Ngāti Kahungunu chair Bayden Barber turned his sights on the government and made the frustration of his iwi towards the coalition government clear.
He said te ao Māori was fed up and sick of what he described as unrelenting, racist attacks on Māori and Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
"Kei te mōhio nei tātou, kei te takahi tonutia rātou, i te Tiriti , i te whakaputanga, te Kiingitanga, ngā kaupapa Māori katoa, ko rātou ka takahi. Nō reira, ae kua māharahara nei ahau, tōku iwi, tātou katoa i ngā mahi hianga, pokokōhua a tēnei kāwanatanga."
"We are all too familiar with their attacks on the Treaty, te whakaputanga, te Kiingitanga, doesn't matter what, if it's Māori, it's a target. So, yes, I am frustrated, my iwi is frustrated, we are all sick and tired of their deception and treachery."
Barber urged Kiingitanga representative Tukoroirangi Morgan to share those sentiments with government representatives expected to attend Koroneihana celebrations later on Friday afternoon.
The prime minister and deputy prime minister would not attend this year's celebrations.

title: Scottish Holocaust victim recognised at Auschwitz
content:
Scottish Holocaust victim recognised at Auschwitz
- Published
The name of a Scot who died in the Holocaust after refusing to abandon Jewish children in her care has been added to a special memorial wall at Auschwitz.
Jane Haining is recognised in a renewed section of the Auschwitz Birkenau Memorial and Museum's main exhibition - devoted to hundreds of prisoners for whom no registration photographs were taken.
The new name plaques adorn the wall of a long corridor and are displayed next to many images of prisoners dressed in striped shirts with shaved heads.
Haining's death certificate said she died in hospital on 17 July 1944, aged 47, but it is widely accepted she died in a gas chamber and her remains are on the Auschwitz site.
- Hungarian march honours Auschwitz Scot - Published14 April 2019

- Auschwitz Scot recalled by former pupil - Published7 June 2017

Born and raised in the village of Dunscore in the south of Scotland, Haining was the matron at a Church of Scotland school in Budapest from 1932 to 1944.
The Scottish Mission School had around 400 day and boarder pupils aged from six to 16 years old, a mixture of Jewish and Christian girls.
The Church of Scotland said she helped keep the children safe for more than four years after the war broke out in 1939.
Despite numerous offers to return home she stayed on, saying: "If these children need me in days of sunshine, how much more do they need me in days of darkness?"
She was arrested by German officers in April 1944 and taken to Auschwitz the following month.
A spokesman for Auschwitz Birkenau Memorial and Museum said: "The corridor has two important purposes.
"It restores individual names and identities to people who were imprisoned and killed in Auschwitz, but it also helps visitors understand the complexity of the prisoner population."
Members of Haining's family - Kevin O'Brien, Liz Harrigan and Patricia Audis - visited the exhibition this week during a study tour to Auschwitz, organised by the Renfrewshire branch of the Unison trade union.
Her neice, Deirdre MacDowell, said: "To see Jane's name on a permanent memorial wall makes one ask how is it that she came to be in Auschwitz?
"And that's the beginning of her story and it can be told to all who ask about her.
"Her story is humbling, full of compassion and kindness and makes us think about how we live our own lives - it is a legacy for us all."
A Church of Scotland spokesman said it was "very moving" to see her name added to the corridor wall to keep her memory alive for "generations to come".
"It is more important than ever that people learn the lessons of history and do not make the mistakes of the past," he said.

title: She gave up her childhood dream of becoming a doctor to fix what doctors cannot
content:
When Dami Oyenekan watched a patient die waiting for care in the emergency ward at the Lagos State University Teaching Hospital (LASUTH), she realised a hard truth: even the best doctors are helpless when the system behind them is broken. Instead of putting on a white coat, she chose to build the infrastructure of medicine. Today, after building quality engineering and AI systems at Medtronic, Cleerly, and Google Health, she leads AI initiatives at GE HealthCare, engineering the exact healthtech solutions she once wished existed. In this week’s edition of My Life in Tech, Dami shares with JOHN ADOYI her journey from witnessing systemic failure in Lagos to building the future of global healthcare and digital records.
In April 2012, 14-year-old Oluwadamilola “Dami” Oyenekan thought she was catching a glimpse of her future.
For years, she had insisted she was going to be a doctor. When Greensprings School, a private school in Lagos, sent its Year 10 students on an “experience week” career placement, Oyenekan knew exactly where she wanted to go.
Her father, however, had a different plan. Rather than placing her in a comfortable private hospital, he insisted she spend her two-week placement at the Lagos State University Teaching Hospital (LASUTH). He wanted her to see the unfiltered reality of public healthcare in Nigeria.
Within two days, Oyenekan was calling her father to pick her up.
It wasn’t that she found medicine too difficult; it was the systemic helplessness. She watched patients wait hours for care while stretched-thin doctors struggled with limited resources. In the emergency ward, she witnessed a patient die while waiting for treatment, followed by the agonizing sight of a doctor comforting the grieving family.
“The person was gone,” Oyenekan recalls.
The tragedy raised a question that would ultimately redirect her life: What happens when even the best doctor lacks the infrastructure to do their job?
“I realized that even if I went to the best medical school and became a top doctor, returning to that same setting meant I couldn’t do my best work without adequate support,” she says. “There were gaps doctors couldn’t fill on their own, gaps where technology could serve as the bridge.”
Finding her true alignment
Despite her realization, Oyenekan still wanted to give medicine a fair shot. She moved to the United Kingdom in 2014 to pursue her studies. During a career talk, she approached a visiting physician and secured a two-week shadowing internship at Maidstone Hospital in Kent.
There, inside an NHS operating room, came her final turning point. While observing a procedure to insert a subdermal implant into a patient’s arm, she had to look away.
“I realised, I can’t look at this. I don’t want to be here,” she says.
The UK had world-class resources, but clinical practice simply was not her calling. She wanted to transform healthcare at a system level.
In 2015, Oyenekan moved to the United States to attend the University of Minnesota. Unlike the British system, the American university curriculum allowed her to explore psychology, biological sciences, and various engineering disciplines before declaring a major.
She eventually found the exact intersection she had been searching for: Bioproducts and Biosystems Engineering, a field that applied advanced engineering principles to biological systems and healthcare delivery.
From campus leader to corporate quality engineer
At Minnesota, Oyenekan built her community through the National Society of Black Engineers (NSBE). Joining in her second year, she rose to Vice President in her third year and Chapter President in her fourth.
Navigating a college where Black students were a small minority, Oyenekan focused on visibility, academic support, and corporate pipelines. Under her presidency, the chapter organized study nights and corporate mentorship programs, winning the university’s Student Group of the Year award for the first time.
Her leadership opened major corporate doors. In 2018, Oyenekan was selected for Genentech’s prestigious G-Links program, which selected roughly 25 students out of 500 applicants nationwide to pair with senior corporate executives. Paired with the company’s Vice President of Quality, Oyenekan spent three months as a regulatory intern, mastering clinical trial documentation, quality engineering, and US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) compliance frameworks.
“That exposed me to quality in biotech,” she says. “It ended up laying the foundation for my entire career.”
By her final year, her work with NSBE paid off again. At an NSBE national conference, where nearly 80% of her attending chapter members secured internships or full-time offers, Oyenekan interviewed with executives from global medical technology giant Medtronic.
Upon graduating in 2019, she joined Medtronic full-time as a Quality Engineer in Sunnyvale, California.
Pivoting from hardware to AI and software
At Medtronic, Oyenekan spent two years in the gastrointestinal and hepatology division, ensuring minimally invasive medical devices met strict FDA regulatory standards.
“Anyone can develop a device,” she explains. “But there are strict requirements around how that device is developed, documented, and traced, from the moment raw components arrive to final testing.”
In 2021, seeking to transition from hardware to software and artificial intelligence, Oyenekan joined Cleerly, a healthtech startup that uses AI to analyse coronary CT scans to detect early heart disease. Over nine months, she adapted her hardware quality engineering framework to suit the fast-paced development cycles of AI healthcare software.
Her work caught the attention of Google Health, which recruited her as a Software Quality Engineer. At Google, she worked on the Automated Retinal Disease Assessment (ARDA) program, an AI tool designed to screen for diabetic retinopathy in low- and middle-income countries across Asia.
The role gave Oyenekan a broader lens, showing her how healthcare technology could be designed and deployed outside Western regulatory ecosystems.
End-to-end impact at GE HealthCare
While at Google, Oyenekan pursued a master’s degree in Medical Product Development Management. Wanting to move beyond quality compliance to shape product strategy, she targeted technical program management.
In May 2023, she joined GE HealthCare as a Technical Program Manager focusing on artificial intelligence. In this role, Oyenekan oversees AI healthcare initiatives end-to-end, managing product development, compliance, and execution simultaneously.
Her work at GE HealthCare has also involved collaboration on global health initiatives supported by the Gates Foundation, providing crucial insights into how large-scale international health projects are deployed.
Returning to the source
Every stage of Oyenekan’s career—from Medtronic and Cleerly to Google and GE HealthCare—has been deliberate preparation for a single goal: returning to address the healthcare infrastructure gaps she first saw as a 14-year-old at LASUTH.
“I want to come back and tackle the lack of infrastructure I witnessed firsthand,” she says.
While optimistic about the promise of AI in African healthcare, Oyenekan emphasises that African nations must not remain passive consumers of technology built elsewhere.
“African countries need to be active participants in that revolution, as opposed to just being on the receiving end,” she stresses. “We need to be involved in generating the data used to build these technologies and shaping the systems around them.”
That conviction centers on digital health infrastructure and data interoperability.
In Nigeria, patients still carry paper folders from hospital to hospital because systems do not talk to one another. Oyenekan advocates for a unified digital health architecture centred on a simple outcome: one patient, one record.
Fourteen years after walking away from clinical medicine at LASUTH, Oyenekan’s journey has come full circle.
“I had one goal, and I initially thought becoming a doctor was the only path to it,” she reflects. “I’m on a different path now, but it’s still leading to the exact same destination.”
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. title: Sportromantiek in Turkse voetbalcompetitie: club met Koerdische identiteit nu bovenaan
content: Voetbalclub Amedspor uit Diyarbakir heeft opnieuw voor een grote verrassing gezorgd in Turkije. De club met een Koerdische identiteit won gisteravond van Besiktas met 3-2 en staat nu zelfs bovenaan in de Turkse competitie. In Diyarbakir en in de regio, in het zuidoosten van het land, werd dat groots gevierd. "Dit is iets om heel trots op te zijn", zegt een fan vlak na de wedstrijd. "Niet alleen voor de inwoners van Diyarbakir, maar voor alle Koerden. Uit Van, Batman, het maakt niet uit. Alle Koerden zijn op dit moment trots op Amedspor." Dat de club nu bovenaan staat is opvallend. In het verleden heeft de club met tegenwerking te maken gehad. Zo werden de fans soms niet toegelaten bij uitwedstrijden. Ook beschikt de club over aanzienlijk minder financiële middelen dan de traditionele topclubs. Ter vergelijking: het budget van Besiktas ligt tien keer hoger. "We zijn in tegenstelling tot andere clubs geen bedrijf, we blijven overeind dankzij de steun van het volk, dankzij de shirts die mensen kopen en dankzij de kaartverkoop", zegt voorzitter Nahit Eren tegen de NOS. Het is volgens velen dan ook een bijzondere prestatie dat deze club als debutant na zes wedstrijden de leiding neemt. Voor sommige fans voelt het alsof ze de competitie hebben gewonnen. Koerdische identiteit Amedspor is nauw verbonden met de Koerdische identiteit, maar supporters benadrukken dat de club voor hen ook staat voor gelijke rechten en vrouwenrechten. Veel Koerden strijden al decennialang lang voor politieke en culturele rechten in Turkije. Winst op het voetbalveld draait dan ook om veel meer dan alleen voetbal. Dat is ook zichtbaar op de tribunes. Twee 22-jarige vrouwen, Berfin Ayder en Evindar Tan van de supportersgroep voor vrouwen Mor Tribun, proberen via de wedstrijden aandacht te vragen voor vrouwenrechten. "Vrouwen worden gedood en lastiggevallen. Als we hier een spandoek ophangen, heeft het een grotere kans internationaal zichtbaar te worden." Volgens Berfin verbroedert sport ook. "We kunnen ook zeggen dat we Koerden zijn, we kunnen Koerdisch spreken. Steeds meer vrouwen sluiten zich bij ons aan, er zijn veel mensen in de omliggende gebieden die betrokken zijn. Er zijn niet alleen Koerdische vrouwen, maar ook Turkse vrouwen die zich aansluiten." Gele zakken Toch zie je soms op de tribunes de spanningen hoog oplopen. Er zijn fans van andere teams met nationalistische opvattingen. Zo is onlangs een supporter in het noordoosten van Turkije op straat aangevallen en liep hij een gebroken neus op omdat hij een tenue van Amedspor aanhad. Ook zijn er de gele plastic zakken op sociale media of op de tribunes. Het is een verwijzing naar de gele zakken waarin lichamen van Koerdische militanten werden vervoerd. Turkije voerde jarenlang een bloedige strijd met de Koerdische PKK waarbij meer dan 40.000 mensen om het leven kwamen. Inmiddels zijn er gesprekken over vrede en ontwapening. Zo houden sommige uitwedstrijden veel meer lading dan een gewone voetbalwedstrijd. De veiligheidsmaatregelen rond wedstrijden zijn daarom ook zwaar. Volgens de voorzitter van Amedspor worden bij een thuiswedstrijd ongeveer 1500 politieagenten en 500 particuliere beveiligers ingezet. Vooroordelen verbroken Tegelijkertijd weet de club ook de harten te raken buiten het overwegend Koerdische Diyarbakir. Mensen uit andere delen van Turkije volgen Amedspor en ook vanuit Europa reizen fans naar de stad. Tijdens de wedstrijd gisteren waren er fans vanuit Nederland en Duitsland. Volgens Eren helpt het sportieve succes in de manier hoe er naar de club wordt gekeken. Het succes van het team leidt ook tot saamhorigheid onder Koerden met uiteenlopende opvattingen. "Eigenlijk worden daardoor bepaalde vooroordelen weggenomen", zegt voorzitter Eren. Op de tribunes zie je soms zelfs Turkse vlaggen wapperen. "Mensen uit de Zwarte Zee-regio, de Egeïsche regio en de Marmara regio volgen Amedspor ook met belangstelling." Een team dat eerder vooral werd gezien als een Koerdisch nationalistische of politiek beladen club, krijgt zo door het succes steeds meer nationale aandacht. En daar ziet de club ook kansen. Eren wil vooral een duurzame club bouwen, gedragen door de gemeenschap. Volgens de 22-jarige Berfin zijn ze er nog lang niet: "Je denkt dat bepaalde vooroordelen zijn weggenomen, maar blijft een een lange weg met obstakels, maar geen onmogelijke."

title: Daughter of ‘pakcik air balang’ carries on her father’s legacy
content:
Ah Yauddin Ahmad died just a month ago, but his youngest daughter does not want the business that supported their family to simply end with him.
She hopes to continue the legacy of her father, better known as “pakcik air balang”, while preserving the recipes and way of doing business she learnt from him growing up.
“I still want to continue because I enjoy it. I want to keep the recipes and the way my father taught me,” the 22-year-old told FMT at her home in Pangsapuri Meru Ehsan here.
Ah Yauddin died on July 18 at age 64 after suffering a lung infection. He became widely known after a video showing him running his stall while caring for his wife at the night market went viral on social media.
Their story touched many hearts. His wife, Roslina Yusuf, had suffered complications from a stroke and diabetes that led to the amputation of her left leg. Yet Ah Yauddin continued to bring her along while he worked.
Roslina died last October after nearly five years of health problems. The couple had been married for almost 40 years.
Now, Nur Aliah is finding the strength to return to the business and expects to reopen her father’s drinks stall next month.
His trading spot at the Taman Datuk Bandar Meru night market has been retained, with payments to the local authority continuing so the business licence remains valid.
Still, Nur Aliah admits the transition will not be easy: her father had previously handled much of the practical side of the business.
“My father used to help with so much. Now I have to learn to do things on my own, including handling the supplies and transport,” she said.
To make this possible, she is working towards getting her driving licence before applying for one that will allow her to drive a van.
For now, she earns some money helping her aunt sell food at night markets around Meru three times a week. Although the income is irregular, she can occasionally earn around RM250 depending on sales.
She also attended courses in kuih-making and baking at GiatMara Klang after receiving an offer from Majlis Amanah Rakyat (Mara).
Even as she prepares to continue her father’s business, Nur Aliah has not given up on another dream: pursuing further studies in early childhood education. She had put her education on hold to care for her parents.
“I still want to continue studying – maybe not now because I still miss my father, but I plan to enter university next year,” she shared.
Looking back on life after losing both parents, Nur Aliah said she had once felt directionless because she had depended so much on her father.
But support from her aunt, her friends and other relatives has helped her find the strength to move forward.
Nur Aliah said she has not received any specific assistance following her father’s death, apart from zakat support that will continue until December.
She hopes to receive educational assistance if she resumes her studies, so she will be able to cover tuition fees and daily living expenses.

title: For Whose Dear Sake Our Fathers Died: Priya Hajela on the trauma, contradictions of colonial history
content:
In the late 1970s and early 80s, in a school hall at The Lawrence School, Sanawar, students would rise together and recite Rudyard Kipling’s “The Children’s Song” — a pledge of loyalty to a motherland, sung in memory of fathers who had died defending it. Scattered through the rows were children who had recently lost fathers of their own, in wars with Pakistan. When the verse about fallen fathers landed, they would cry, and they would leave the hall. Priya Hajela, then a student at the school, never forgot it. “It made a huge impact on me,” she says.
Decades later, that hymn gave her the title of her new novel. For Whose Dear Sake Our Fathers Died, published by Speaking Tiger, follows four generations of the Uppal family across nearly a century of upheaval, beginning after the death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and ending before the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
Speaking to The Indian Express, Hajela says her working title was Battle Lines, but once she finished the manuscript, she realised the book’s emotional charge was the relationship between fathers and sons. “The title has to touch the heart,” she says.
Hajela came to fiction rather late in life after a corporate career spanning 22 years. At 48, she pursued an MFA in creative writing at Goddard College in Vermont, which she completed in 2017, leading her to excavate the histories of her family and her people.
Born in Punjab, she was sent to boarding school at a young age and then moved to the United States at 17. Growing up, she could read Gurmukhi, but could not speak Punjabi fluently.
Her intention, she says, was never to study history for its own sake. “What drives me is actually to get an understanding of who I am and where I come from.”
Story continues below this ad
For Whose Dear Sake Our Fathers Died is a prequel to her earlier novel Ladies’ Tailor, which dealt with the aftermath of 1947. This time, the story is told through Beant Kaur as she pieces together the half-remembered life of her grandfather, Balwant Singh Uppal. “History talks about the leaders,” she said. “It doesn’t talk about what happened to the common man.”
A father’s death, a son’s dilemma
Balwant is where the novel’s central contradiction lives. He despises the East India Company as an “evil force,” but is willing to die for a British officer he personally serves.
The Calcutta army killed Balwant’s own father, a force made up overwhelmingly of Indian troops fighting under British command, says Hajela. “He wonders, are they my enemy, or are the British my enemy?” she says. “Yes, the British were leading, but there were so few of them.”
With the Sikh army his father died fighting for now dismantled, and farming crushed under rising taxes, joining the British Indian Army was the only option for Balwant.
Story continues below this ad
Hajela recounts the anguish of the Ferozepur Regiment, where Sikh soldiers were ordered to fight rebels who looked and spoke like them. They were so similar that they tore their turbans off, only to be torn apart on the battlefield. She says soldiers would turn their faces away as rebels were tied to cannons and blown apart. “There was definitely this massive guilt,” she said. “Is it really necessary? Yes, they rebelled. But to go to this length?”
Reading against the record
Getting the texture of this period right meant refusing to trust any single account, Hajela said. History written by the winners reads differently from history written by the losers, and until Independence, she points out, Indians lost at nearly every turn: the 1857 uprising, both Anglo-Sikh wars.
She found Indian-authored histories often eager to recover heroes and martyrs, while British accounts carried the victors’ biases, and she read the two against each other. Amarpal Singh’s histories of the first and second Anglo-Sikh wars became a key source; Singh, a computer engineer by training who became absorbed in this history, has also traced Sikh war memorials standing today in French fields from the First World War.
For the on-the-ground reality of 1857—what it actually felt like inside the Lucknow residency during the siege—Hajela turned to diaries written by British women, texts she found freely available.
Story continues below this ad
When the narrator doesn’t know everything
With all that research, Hajela’s first draft read like “a history textbook.” Her fix was to strip the story down to Balwant’s own limited vantage point.
“He does not know the rationale, and he does not know what’s happening elsewhere,” she says. “He is observing what is happening before him. And that is what he’s going to tell his granddaughter.”
She draws a direct line to her next project, a work of non-fiction on the Sikh Gurus. Guru Gobind Singh died in 1707, she said, but the Suraj Prakash, the chronicle by Kavi Santokh Singh that documents his life, was not written until the early 1800s.
For a century in between, the stories survived only by being retold and performed, gaining and shedding details with each telling. Hajela insists that the absence of a contemporaneous written record doesn’t make those stories less true.
Story continues below this ad
What’s left to fight for
Asked what she hopes readers take from the book, Hajela hopes it is the idea to “open your eyes, be aware, and find something to stand behind.”
She says the recent Gen Z student protests in Delhi against paper leaks were an example of the kind of stories worth telling.
“The world is becoming really strange,” she said. “You can’t just coast. Believe in something and believe strongly, and then do something for that cause.”
It’s advice Balwant himself gives his grandson in the novel: there may be no grand battles left to fight, but that doesn’t mean inaction is an option.
Story continues below this ad
Whether that instinct to act and pass the story on will survive in a generation fixated on their phones rather than a grandfather’s chair, Hajela isn’t sure. But she hopes the book does what that hymn in the Sanawar Hall once did to her: land somewhere and start a conversation.

title: Indigenous 'turtle women' help save endangered freshwater turtles in the Amazon
content:
On the banks of the Aguarico River in the Ecuadorian Amazon, a group of Indigenous Siekopai women are combining traditional knowledge and modern technology to help a threatened native turtle recover.
Their efforts center around charapa turtles (Podocnemis unifilis), also known as the yellow-spotted Amazon River turtle, Mongabay Latam’s Astrid Arellano reported. The animal’s populations have declined due to hunting adult turtles, harvesting eggs from nests, and pollution from garbage, oil, and gasoline.
“Sometimes we see plastic, garbage bags,” Janeth Piaguaje, a Siekopai community leader of the project, told Mongabay Latam. “We also see dead animals floating down the river. We can’t control all of that, but we do make a significant effort to clean the beaches where we work.”
Boat traffic is also eroding riverbanks, and climate change has caused water levels to rise, flooding the flats where turtles make their nests. Charapa turtles are listed as vulnerable by the IUCN, the global conservation authority.
To help the turtles recover, a group of seven Siekopai women, who call themselves Tari Nomiowa’i, or “turtle women,” patrol the riverbanks looking for turtle tracks and nests. When they find nests, the women carefully collect the eggs, a skill Piaguaje said she learned from her father.
“He taught me how to handle the eggs, how to see on what dates and in what months the turtles lay their nests,” she said.
The women document the date, time, location, and number of eggs in each nest using the Epicollect5 app, a field data collection tool.
Then they take the eggs to an incubation facility where they are protected from predators, flooding, and pollution. Once the eggs hatch, the women continue to care for the baby turtles for another month, feeding them cassava, sweet potato, and taro leaves.
Their painstaking work has paid off.
Over the 2025-26 nesting season, the women collected 235 eggs and successfully hatched and released 208 hatchlings into the Aguarico River over March and April this year. The group invited the local community, including schoolchildren, to participate in the turtle release and attend workshops.
“A little girl said, ‘I’m going to take care of them, I’m going to tell them not to touch the eggs,’” Piaguaje recalled.
A driving force behind the work of the Tari Nomiowa’i is their culture and the ancestral belief that the turtles are a link between the visible and spiritual worlds, each swimming with protection from Koouwajëo, the spiritual chief, mother, and ancestral guardian of the turtles.
“I want Koouwajëo to be proud,” said Piaguaje. “When we protect turtles, we don’t just care for a species; we honor the spirits of the river, strengthen our culture, and maintain the sacred pact between our community and nature.”

title: Sacks, Matkas & Bows Become Sports Gear at Madhya Pradesh’s Baiga Olympics
content: There are no synthetic tracks here. No floodlit stadium. No branded jerseys, expensive sports shoes or professional training camps. Instead, there are gunny sacks, earthen pots, ropes, bows and arrows, mud, wooden sticks and the physical skills that have travelled through generations of the Baiga community. In Baihar, in Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district, these everyday objects become sporting equipment during the Baiga Olympics — a tribal sporting and cultural festival designed around the traditional games of the Baiga people. The event was first organised in Baihar in 2015 by the Balaghat Tourism Promotion Council, with the stated aim of showcasing traditional Baiga games and helping conserve the community’s cultural heritage. Later editions have brought together Baiga participants from Madhya Pradesh and neighbouring states. A 2020 edition, for instance, was planned over three days and invited Baiga communities from parts of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Jharkhand and Andhra Pradesh. But who are the Baigas? The Baigas are one of Madhya Pradesh's Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs)-a special category created to identify tribal communities facing particularly severe socio-economic and infrastructural disadvantages. India currently recognises 75 PVTGs across 18 states and the Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The classification has historically been based on indicators including low literacy, economic vulnerability, geographical isolation, dependence on subsistence livelihoods, and stagnant or declining population trends. The Baiga are among the PVTGs listed in Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. The term itself has an important history. These communities were earlier officially referred to as “Primitive Tribal Groups”, but the terminology was changed to PVTG in 2006–07 because the word “primitive” was considered inappropriate and value-laden. They have traditionally lived in close relationship with the forests of central India, particularly across areas of Madhya Pradesh and neighbouring Chhattisgarh. In Madhya Pradesh, large concentrations of the community are found in districts including Mandla and Balaghat. Their relationship with the forest goes well beyond livelihood. Baiga communities have traditionally depended on forest resources for food, medicine and other necessities, while maintaining extensive knowledge of local plants and their uses. And then there are the games. Long before the word "Olympics" was attached to them, many of these activities were simply part of community life. The Baiga Olympics takes those games out of the village setting and puts them into a common arena. So, what exactly happens at the Baiga Olympics? The answer is wonderfully different from what one might expect from a conventional sporting meet. Take Bora Daud. Instead of sprinting down a professional track, participants climb into gunny sacks and race. The humble sack becomes the equivalent of a piece of sporting equipment. Then there is the Matka race, where participants race while balancing earthen pots. It turns an everyday object into a test of balance, coordination and speed. From Matka Daud and Bora Daud to Bhalafenk, Dhanushbaan, Kabaddi and Kho-Kho, the games blend tradition with sport. Photograph: (Madhya Pradesh Tourism/Shutterstock) Bhalafenk, or spear throwing, draws on the physical precision associated with traditional hunting skills. Dhanushbaan, involving the bow and arrow, is another important traditional contest. The Madhya Pradesh government lists it among the Baiga Olympics' traditional "hunter games". There is also Vajni Khel, described as a traditional form of wrestling; Rassa-Kashi, the tug-of-war; and running events including relay and Tritangi races. The official list of competitions has included Matka Daud, Bora Daud, Tritangi race, relay race, Bhalafenk, Vajni Khel, Lipa-Poti, kabaddi, kho-kho, volleyball, Rassa-Kashi and Dhanushbaan. Earlier editions have also featured games such as Gobardanda. What do you need to compete? Not much by modern sporting standards. A sack for Bora Daud. An earthen pot for the Matka race. A spear for Bhalafenk. And, most importantly, the knowledge of how to use them. A special torch also forms part of the event. According to the Balaghat district administration, the torch travels through different districts before reaching Baihar, with a promotional vehicle accompanying it and inviting Baiga youth to participate. The event was first organised in Baihar in 2015 by the Balaghat Tourism Promotion Council. Photograph: (Government of Madhya Pradesh) The participants, too, are not necessarily professional athletes. The Ministry of Tourism describes the event as one where both young and older members of the Baiga community can participate, rather than restricting competition to trained athletes. A participant does not need years of specialised coaching, a sponsorship deal or access to a stadium. A skill learned through community life can become the basis for competition. Why does something like this matter? Because indigenous cultures can disappear quietly. The Baiga Olympics offers one way of keeping some of those practices visible. People from Baiga community are all set to welcome you to take a sneak peek into their world with Baiga Olympics, Balaghat. The 3 day fiesta from 4th-6th Jan will showcase the rich culture of Baiga tribes of Madhya Pradesh.#MPTourism pic.twitter.com/nsFQWyLVUD — Madhya Pradesh Tourism (@MPTourism) January 2, 2020 There is also an important question of dignity. For years, tribal communities have often been represented primarily through poverty, remoteness or deprivation. The Baiga Olympics attempts to shift the frame. An Olympics without an Olympic-sized budget That may ultimately be the most compelling part of the Baiga Olympics. The event borrows the language and spectacle of a global sporting competition, the torch, competitions, teams, spectators and prizes but changes the meaning of what counts as an athlete and what counts as sport. The Baiga Olympics does not attempt to reproduce the world's Olympics in a forested corner of Madhya Pradesh. It builds a sporting platform around what the community already knows.
