title: Residents say Philippines’ Pax Silica Hub will force them off their ancestral land
content:
CAPAS, Philippines - Children’s laughter and the gentle sound of a flowing river are the daily accompaniment to life in a hamlet of about 200 indigenous Aeta families, but members of the community told Radio Free Asia they are in danger of losing their idyllic way of life because a planned U.S.-led tech hub will force them to relocate.
The majority of the residents of Sapang Kawayan, about 47 miles (75 kilometers) north of Manila, are not formally schooled, but they are educated by the ways of nature. Farming cycles are dictated by the monsoon season, and at all times, they are at the whims of a nearby volcano, Mount Pinatubo.
The Philippine government has approved the construction of the Pax Silica hub on a 4,000-acre (1,619 hectare) area inside New Clark City, on land that was part of the U.S. military reservation that included Clark Air Base until the area was returned to the Philippines government in 1991.
Families in the village have already received a letter from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) informing them they must relocate from the village because it is included in the development plan, Casamira Capiz Maniego, a 72-year-old Aeta resident of Sapang Kawayan, told RFA.
“They should just have us killed because we will fight for our land,” Maniego said. “We have lived for generations in the mountains long before the Americans came. What will happen to us if they take our land?”
Economic and strategic boon
Defense analysts view the 14-country Pax Silica initiative as a symbolic return of the Americans to their former base in the Philippines, Washington’s staunchest ally in the region. But more than that, it is viewed as a plan to keep semiconductor and AI facilities under one U.S.-controlled roof as Beijing rolls out its own, similar initiative.
The larger geopolitical context, however, is not lost on observers, with Manila needing the support of Washington as it faces territorial threats from China, America’s chief rival in the region.
Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has touted the project as one that would “revitalize” the country’s economy and create “quality jobs” for the people. Marcos and top officials have downplayed concerns over potential impacts to the water table and the environment, and fears that the hub would hand too much control to Washington.
“I cannot see how another country can come into the Philippines and, for example, exploit our minerals without the agreement of our Philippine government,” Marcos said in August at a forum organized by the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines.
The Pax Silica hub will enable the Philippines to process minerals locally instead of exporting ore, Marcos said, adding that once realized, it would be “the Philippines fully exploiting our own treasure, our own national treasure, our own natural resources.”
Many people concerned over the environmental and social impact of the project have organized protests, including one earlier this month, where five paralegals were arrested and nearly 30 others were detained while rallying outside a hotel that had been hosting a business forum about Pax Silica.
Regarding the displacement of the Aetas, the affected area sits roughly within 10 hectares (24 acres) of the 1,600-hectare site, BCDA President and CEO Joshua M. Bingcang told media, including Philippine outlet ABS-CBN, on Monday. He said any relocations would affect an estimated 200 people in 40 households, and they would stay within the same jurisdiction.
“They will not be displaced,” Bingcang said. “They will just be pushed a little bit but they will still be in the same barangay, the same community, the same BCDA land.”
Historical rights?
The Aetas have lived in the rough hinterlands as far back as they can remember, but it was in the 1850s during the Spanish colonial era that authorities formally recognized their presence in decrees, which the Aetas now view as historical proof of their occupation of the land.
Tribal elders believe that even without any piece of paper, the government should recognize their “ancestral domain.”
Spain later ceded the islands to the U.S. and during the time that the Philippines was a U.S. territory, Washington considered the Aetas to be nomadic peoples, displacing many to build Clark Air Base.
The Aetas are gentle hunter-gatherers and crop farmers who generally avoid conflict, Maniego said. They have learned over many years how to co-exist with the “lowlanders,” – what they call Filipinos who live in nearby cities and towns – with some Aeta even working outside of their tiny mountain communities alongside the lowlanders.
Visiting the tribal area is like being transported to an entirely different world, where the trappings of modern-day life are absent. Barefoot children walked on the dirt, while a herd of swamp water buffaloes grazed in the distance. The occasional hum of a motorcycle buzzed nearby as an Aeta caravan carrying wood charcoal slowly negotiated the muddy trail.
Private security guards hired by the BCDA blocked the dirt roads to Maniego’s village, however. RFA managed to reach one remote area by passing through small dirt roads accompanied by three social workers.
Tribal leader Petronila Capiz, 63, argued that their ancestral land was crucial to their story as a people, their heritage and the continued survival of the Aetas. The land, she said, has been passed down from one generation to the next.
People, water, and land
Allowing the government to erect a facility here would be a death knell to their way of life, Capiz said, adding that government surveyors have already been spotted measuring the land and studying the Bangot River, the community’s primary source of water and sustenance.
“It will destroy the environment and our source of water, the Bangot River, where we also fish,” she said. “Water and land, without these we will die. Nature has given us these, and they will just destroy it for the sake of Pax Silica.”
Capiz’ cousin, Nelson de Guzman, 57, was emotional. His weather-beaten face was covered in sweat as he called on fellow Filipinos for support against the multimillion project.
Pax Silica, he said, is like “a gigantic leech that will suck the life out of the soil and mountain.” De Guzman is volunteering to organize tribal communities in other areas to express solidarity with their cause.
“We will resist and fight for our rights,” he stressed. “We are not just fighting for ourselves individually, but for the entire tribe.”
Edited by Eugene Whong. Jojo Riñoza contributed to this report from Capas.

title: In Texas, a historic Route 66 neighborhood taps its deep roots for a revival
content:
In Texas, a historic Route 66 neighborhood taps its deep roots for a revival
Loading...
| Amarillo, Texas
David Rosas turns off Arthur Avenue and starts walking through the old Mexican American Barrio of his childhood.
The first landmark is an empty lot.
His grandmother’s house once stood here, Mr. Rosas says. It was a place where relatives streamed in and out, coffee seemed always to be brewing, and everyone came to learn the family news. He has called it the family’s “bank, library, meeting place.”
Why We Wrote This
Many American neighborhoods carry the history of the people who built them and helped them flourish. When time erodes the bonds that define a place, new energy can help a place like the Barrio in Amarillo, Texas, renew itself.
He remembers the railroad men walking home for lunch, then heading back to work. Afterward, his grandmother and a neighbor would pull out flour, water, and lard and begin making tortillas, the kitchen filling with the familiar rhythm of the rolling pins.
“I wish I could hear it right now,” he says. Walking down the street a few blocks, he passes a funeral home. But Mr. Rosas knows the building by an older name: El Salón Mexicano.
His grandfather, Mateo Lopez, a Santa Fe railroad worker, helped build the neighborhood hall with other residents in the 1930s as a place for dances, weddings, and quinceañeras. “The Barrio is a town within a town,” Mr. Rosas says. “We didn’t travel far.”
The short walk amounts to a century of Barrio history, a story about how American communities are made, and often remade in order to endure. In the late 19th century, Mexican railroad workers, brought in through programs of the Santa Fe Railway, arrived with their families and built homes, businesses, and a Catholic church – a world within a world, shaped partly by the segregation and discrimination that kept them apart from much of the city’s wider civic life. But the Barrio can be seen, too, as a recognizable American story of frontier towns in which neighbors helped out neighbors, and civic services became a fully communal affair.
Like so many small towns along Route 66, old boundaries have loosened, and families have scattered as regional economies reshape where people work and live. But the neighborhood is being rebuilt again. Their challenge is no longer how to create a community within those boundaries, but how to carry forward the belonging that grew there.
There is a Route 66 irony embedded in the Barrio’s story. Its 10th Avenue was part of the original highway in 1926 – the road Americans would celebrate as the “Main Street of America.” It was rerouted north in 1932.
Yet on the other side of Amarillo’s railroad tracks, Mexican American families kept building their version of the Main Street ideal: businesses, places to gather, familiar families, and a commitment to one another.
■ ■ ■
For Mr. Rosas, that older Main Street can be measured less in storefronts than in relationships.
“Back then when you met somebody, an elderly gentleman, they asked you who your parents were,” he says. He would give his name, and the older man would begin placing him.
Lupe’s son. Mateo’s grandson. Then would come the stories: Your father helped me with this. I knew your grandfather. “Being recognized by your parents and your grandparents, it’s a big deal,” Mr. Rosas says. “I mean, it carried weight.”
His grandfather was one of the first pillars of the Barrio. His father, Lupe Rosas, carried that ethic into a different era. A World War II veteran who later worked at Amarillo’s veterans hospital, he was one of the first members of the NAACP. In the 1950s, he and two Catholic priests conducted a sit-in at one of Amarillo’s whites-only restaurants.
Lupe also became one of the people neighbors sought out when they did not know how to navigate institutions beyond the Barrio. Someone needed help with a Social Security form. Someone had a problem with the city. Someone needed to know whom to ask.
“When people had problems, nobody had a lawyer,” says Mr. Rosas, who dropped out of school in the eighth grade and went on to spend four decades selling cars. “My dad could figure something out. And I do that for a lot of people.”
Mr. Rosas holds no public office. But neighbors call him when trash is not picked up or a dilapidated property becomes a problem. He goes to city meetings, pushes officials for neighborhood investment, and says Amarillo’s current mayor takes his calls.
People sometimes call him the “mayor of the Barrio.” Mr. Rosas has given himself an arguably grander title, printed on his business card: H.M.I.C. – “Head Mexican in Charge.”
His charm and levity, however, belie his seriousness. In 2017 he became part of a neighborhood revitalization process.
For him, the effort is about more than getting sidewalks or city money. His grandmother’s house is gone. Relatives have scattered across Amarillo and beyond. Mr. Rosas himself lives about five miles from the Barrio.
The old social geography is harder to see. “It’s getting lost,” he says.
■ ■ ■
Teresa Kenedy turns off Arthur Avenue onto 10th and drives slowly toward the railroad tracks, narrating the Barrio almost block by block.
There are the murals marking the entrance to the old neighborhood. Then the new trees. Banners celebrating Día de los Muertos with sugar skulls. Street lamps. Bike racks. Nine street benches painted in reds, blues, and greens. Most noticeably, there are sidewalks – wide, wheelchair accessible stretches of concrete in a neighborhood where, away from the businesses, sidewalks are scarce.
“What you’re seeing – none of that was here prior to April of this year,” says Ms. Kenedy, now the president of The Barrio Neighborhood Planning Committee, on which Mr. Rosas serves, too. For the old main street, it amounts to a $6.1 million makeover the organization helped facilitate.
But Ms. Kenedy does not describe the project as an attempt to make 10th Avenue look new. She talks instead about making the street announce where it is – and what came before.
For Mr. Rosas, the Barrio is an inheritance. He can walk its streets through generations of his own family. His argument for rebuilding the neighborhood begins with memory, but becomes a claim on the larger city: “We’ve paid taxes forever,” he says. “I want some of that money back here.”
Ms. Kenedy’s attachment is chosen. She did not grow up in the Barrio, but in tiny Snowville, Utah, near the Idaho state line, where hers was the only Hispanic family for about 20 miles. Her father died when she was age 2, leaving her mother to raise seven children. Ms. Kenedy says everyone chipped in; she began working at age 9, first as a babysitter and then as a dishwasher.
She arrived in the Amarillo area for college at age 20, studying to be a social worker, “connecting people with resources.”
Her biography appears almost geographically during the drive. She passes Caprock High School, where she worked for 13 years in drug prevention, and then Bowie Middle School, where she spent another seven.
Then she became the coordinator of a federally funded program to place the children of migrant farmworkers in school, even though they might remain for only weeks or months before their families moved on.
When she retired in 2015, Ms. Kenedy, a widow with no children, committed to volunteering in the Barrio, her home for over 45 years.
Together, she and Mr. Rosas represent the challenge facing the Barrio now. The first generations built a community from the ground up. Their descendants inherited its stories and obligations. The work of this generation is different: to turn that inheritance into something sturdy enough to survive change.
In 2018, Ms. Kenedy became something of the Barrio’s historian. She led a task force that interviewed older residents for a book that would preserve the neighborhood’s collective memory.
She conducted many of the interviews herself. When the group needed someone to turn the interviews into a book and nobody volunteered, Ms. Kenedy did that, too.
The book was also part of the committee’s effort to put together a historical map. The map and the memories fed into a neighborhood plan.
And the plan, eventually, became the trees, benches, and lights along 10th Avenue.
Memory, in other words, became infrastructure.
■ ■ ■
More than a century after an earlier generation built El Salón Mexicano because the Barrio needed somewhere to gather, Mr. Rosas and Ms. Kenedy are trying to create another such place – not to restore the confining boundaries of the old neighborhood, but to give its communal life a place to flourish again.
The group calls it La Plazita. Right now it’s an empty lot, but they are planning to turn it into a community park with a stage. Mr. Rosas was the one who spotted the property for sale. The city ultimately acquired it and deeded it to the planning committee.
For now, there is a mural, several benches, sponsored paving stones, and a storage building. Ms. Kenedy envisions a performance stage, food trucks, mariachi musicians, folklórico dancers, pop-up markets, movie nights, quinceañeras, and wedding receptions. There will be free Wi-Fi. The committee has already begun holding events on the unfinished lot so people will get used to coming there.
As she walks through the unfinished La Plazita, she also mentions the legacy of Mateo Lopez.
“Here’s someone who came as a young man with his wife from Mexico to the United States, came to Amarillo, helped build this railroad, helped build a community center – and his grandson is now helping renovate this neighborhood. It came full circle, right?”

title: Desde 2025, Chiapas ha alfabetizado a 250 mil personas
content:
Viernes 11 de septiembre de 2026, p. 13
San Cristóbal de Las Casas, Chis., Galardonado con el Premio Internacional de Alfabetización Confusio de la Organización de Naciones Unidas para la Educación, la Ciencia y la Cultura (Unesco) 2026, el programa estatal Chiapas Puede ha logrado enseñar a leer y escribir a 250 mil personas en los 124 municipios de la entidad, en su mayoría indígenas, de 2025 a la fecha, informó Flor Marina Bermúdez, coordinadora del proyecto.
En entrevista con La Jornada, la funcionaria destacó que en promedio se destinan cada año 850 millones de pesos a la entrega de la beca Rosario Castellanos, con la que se garantizan 4 mil pesos a cada beneficiario que logra aprender a leer y escribir. Este apoyo, dijo, “es una de las acciones más efectivas para lograr que quienes no han tenido la oportunidad de escolarizarse puedan alfabetizarse”.
Indicó que por medio de un “modelo propio e innovador” de alfabetización desarrollado por el programa, que incluye la elaboración de los materiales didácticos a partir de las lenguas maternas de los alfabetizados, “hemos logrado una elevada tasa de éxito”. Enfatizó que actualmente se atiende a miles de indígenas de los cincos principales grupos lingüísticos en el estado: tseltal, tsotsil, chol, zoque y tojolabal.
Luego de ser reconocido por la Unesco como uno de los seis proyectos de alfabetización más innovadores del mundo, Bermúdez señaló que se buscó recuperar las mejores prácticas de alfabetización en América Latina para los pueblos indígenas y afrodescendientes, y “de la mano de alfabetizadores indígenas y con la visión de las etnopedagogías, coincidimos en hacer algo innovador: elaborar primero los materiales en lenguas indígenas y luego en español”.
Por ello, dijo, los libros que se usan en las comunidades no son traducciones, sino “textos auténticamente hechos por autores indígenas, que parten de la cosmovisión de los pueblos originarios, utilizando ejemplos que son comunes a éstos y las gramáticas del lenguaje, que hacen que los educandos puedan aprender primero en su lengua y luego en español”.
Se beneficiaron 165 mil mujeres
Agregó que este modelo de alfabetización ya impactó a 165 mil mujeres, en su mayoría indígenas, quienes representan 80 por ciento del total de la población que se ha logrado alfabetizar en la administración del gobernador Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar.
Precisó que en el estado se tenían detectadas entre 340 y 380 mil personas no alfabetizadas, por lo que para el año próximo se tiene la meta de alcanzar a otros 100 mil habitantes.

title: What te reo Māori taught me about the Irish language I never learned
content: I was told that Gaeilge was a language of the past. Learning about te reo Māori showed me what had really been taken from us – and what it means to fight for a language’s future. Growing up in Ireland, I attended a rural school with fewer than 60 pupils. Every morning, we’d clasp our sticky hands together and thrum the Lord’s Prayer. When the teacher called the roll, each child would say “anseo”, which means here – the first Gaeilge, or traditional Irish, word I learned. My teachers and family told me Gaeilge was a dead language; not a vital part of our heritage, but an inconvenient hour stuffed between maths and the lunch break. It was something we only needed to learn enough of to pass our exams. I spent years matching the shapes of the words to each other, never truly understanding their meaning. It wasn’t until I was here in Aotearoa, on the other side of the world, that I realised I grew up less than an hour away from one of Ireland’s strongest Gaeltacht regions, in which the community speaks primarily in Gaeilge. My language was still very much alive and I could have been a part of it. When I feel the weight of this missed opportunity, it makes me want to scream loud enough to wake my younger self up. When I was contemplating learning te reo Māori, I was hesitant because of my lack of Gaeilge. How could I ask someone to teach me their reo and expect them to trust that I would honour their language when I hadn’t honoured my own? This week is the 51st Wiki o Te Reo Māori. Ireland has had Seachtain na Gaeilge (Irish Language Week) since 1902. September here, March there, both held at the beginning of spring, breathing in new life and uplifting the languages. Our cultures are both deeply embedded in language, land and whakapapa. We were both colonised by the same country and, in some situations, the same people played roles in the colonisation of both countries. Some of the legislation used by the British in Ireland was implemented here, and the same tools of oppression used on the Irish were employed against Māori, including by some Irish settlers. Our timelines weave across each other like bruised rushes. Te tiriti was signed only six years before the Irish famine began. We often only understand the colonisation of a country in the language of the coloniser, which prevents us from understanding the depth of grief, horror and significance of the pain caused. If we talk about a mountain or river being bought, sold or stolen in English, it means something entirely different to hearing the same story in te reo from a Māori person speaking of how their tipuna, their ancestor, was bought, sold or stolen. Just as it is impossible to represent in English what certain sacred Irish landmarks hold – the centuries of story, memories and meaning that are embedded in the language we use to speak about them cannot be replicated in the language of those who tried to rip it all away from us. Bilingual Gaelige road signs in Creggs, County Galway. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons) Irish Ogham inscriptions date back to the 4th century, while te reo Māori came from the Polynesian languages brought to Aotearoa from Hawaiki, arriving here around the 13th century. Our languages sustained us for centuries; they were how we expressed what we understood about the land, what to plant and when. As the late Manchán Magan wrote, the Irish have 32 words for a field, because we needed that many. Similarly in te reo, there are at least 30 names for different types of oneone or soils. Our languages thrived until the English got involved. In the 1700s, while the Crown dug its claws into Ireland – destroying our Brehon legal system and enforcing English as the main language – James Cook was arriving on the shores of Aotearoa. Systematically, the native languages were pushed to the peripheries and associated with being rural and uneducated, while English was associated with prosperity. Education was used as a weapon against both languages. Systematic physical and psychological abuse of indigenous children literally beat the language out of them and their homes. But it wasn’t violence that posed the biggest threat, it was shame. In Aotearoa, students were beaten for speaking Māori in front of their classes and whānau. In Ireland, children were made to wear a bata scóir or tally stick around their necks. Every time they spoke Gaeilge, a notch would be added to the stick – the number of notches determining their punishment. Shame like that lasts generations, and produces adults who protect their children by denying them their indigenous language. The history of both Ireland and Aotearoa is scarred from the words torn from our ancestors’ mouths. An aching gap remains inside us as we try to reclaim what should never have been taken. After the Republic of Ireland reclaimed its independence, Gaeilge was declared the country’s first official language in 1937. It became compulsory to learn it in school. However, the north of Ireland remains under British rule and people there continue to fight to keep the Gaeilge language alive. In 1987, te reo Māori became an official language of Aotearoa after the Waitangi Tribunal found te reo was a taonga protected under te tiriti. Both countries reached a turning point when citizens focused on ensuring children could learn the languages again. This began healing the fractures between generations that had been unable to pass down their language. Kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa in Aotearoa, and gaelscoileanna in Ireland, were started by groups of parents and activists. Conradh na Gaeilge or the Gaelic League, the Gaeltacht civil rights movement in Ireland, the Māori language petition and Te Reo Māori Society of Wellington played essential roles in uplifting and sustaining our languages. Ireland launched its first indigenous-language radio station, Raidió na Gaeltachta, in 1972, which was followed by iwi radio in 1987 in Aotearoa. TV stations came in the 1990s and 2000s: TG4 in Ireland and Whakaata Māori in Aotearoa. This helped bring the languages into present, daily life, beaming them into homes across the countries. Te reo Māori is ebbing and flowing like the tides. (Image: Getty; additional design: Archi Banal) Still, the fight continues. Beyond these key moments, there have been ongoing, constant threats to the languages, and millions of people who have fought and fight, daily against these threats. According to Unesco, the world loses a language every two weeks, with at least 40% of the world’s 7,000 languages considered endangered. Gaeilge and te reo Māori continue to stand. As time goes on, both languages have progressed into digital and mainstream media, with music providing one of the most significant revival efforts. Jordyn with a Why, Te Kahureremoa, Stan Walker and Marlon Williams in Aotearoa and Roís, Kneecap and Seo Linn in Ireland are all artists proudly uplifting their reo, laying a path for others to follow. Irish signage features place names in Gaeilge first with English second. It grounds you in place, reminding you that you’re on indigenous land that some asshole tried to rename. The current president of Ireland, Catherine Connolly, made Gaeilge a central feature of her election campaign and won by a landslide. The Irish government is targeting 20% of public sector recruits to be Gaeilge-competent by 2030 as part of its ambition to become a fully bilingual public service. Meanwhile in Aotearoa, the current government has aggressively stripped back reo in public institutions, with English being prioritised over Māori. Significant money and time has been spent securing English as an official language despite the move being widely criticised. This led to Green MP Tamatha Paul’s viral kōrero in which she called English a “bastard language” and questioned why the “snowflakes” in charge can’t cope with hearing a language outside of their own. While it’s easy to think te reo is only being bludgeoned, there are also people working hard to uplift it. Those teaching their mokopuna, joining kura reo, signing petitions, speaking te reo at home and work, supporting their whānau. Grassroots community groups continue their mahi. Maihi Karauna – the Crown’s Māori Language Strategy – has committed to working towards one million people being able to speak conversational Māori by 2040 and 85% of Aotearoa to value te reo as a key part of its national identity. It’s our responsibility asIrish here in Aotearoa to help provide Māori protection over their reo. We don’t get to be racist and Irish, and we don’t get to be Irish living on colonised land without honouring its history, people and language. To live as te tiriti partners, we need to understand each other, and that begins with language. We don’t need to learn te reo to do this, but we do need to show it our respect. More Reading

title: 13yo Mount Isa bull rider sets sights on Texas
content:
Mount Isa Rodeo backs next generation of outback stars
In short:
The Mount Isa Rodeo is backing the next generation of outback riders, committing $10,000 to help 13-year-old Lareece Daley-Kennedy compete at two youth world finals in the United States.
The Kalkadoon and Pitta Pitta cowgirl is among several young North West riders making their mark as the revived rodeo puts greater focus on developing local talent.
What's next?
Lareece will travel to the United States to compete in youth world finals in Oklahoma and Texas.
Inside the Kalkadoon Arena, in the heart of Queensland's wild north-west, courage can be measured in eight seconds.
The Mount Isa Rodeo is the biggest in the Southern Hemisphere and this year some of its youngest riders made the biggest impression.
Kalkadoon and Pitta Pitta cowgirl Lareece Daley-Kennedy, 13, is preparing to step onto the international stage after receiving invitations to two youth world finals in the United States.
She has been invited to compete at the Professional Youth Roughstock Association World Finals in Oklahoma and the World Championship Mini Bulls World Finals in Texas.
The invitations follow a string of strong performances across the North West, including a second-place finish on her first steer ride earlier this year.
At this year's Mount Isa Rodeo she came just short of the buzzer in the Mount Isa round before returning to place third in the Indigenous mini bulls.
Now the Mount Isa Rodeo is putting real weight behind that next generation, committing $10,000 to help get Lareece to the United States.
It is the first time the incumbent board has directly backed a young rider in this way.
For Lareece, the secret to lasting eight seconds is simple.
"Just lock your knees in and your legs and just hold on," she said.
Lareece was not the only young rider to impress.
Cloncurry brothers Dallas and Ashley Murphy, aged 10 and 14, swept the mini bull titles.
Cade Ferguson, 19, was crowned the rodeo's all-round cowboy, just weeks after becoming world champion in bull riding and reserve world champion in saddle bronc at the Cinch World Championship Junior Rodeo in Oklahoma.
In her father's footsteps
Lareece took up riding after hearing stories about her father Nathan Kennedy's own days in the sport.
"I just wanted to follow my dad's footsteps," she said.
The sport has taught her how to take a hard landing and get back up.
Earlier this year she was winded on her first steer ride and last year at Cloncurry she was thrown and landed on her neck.
"I'd heard people say, 'Oh, she came second', and I just got up like nothing happened," she said.
Her family initially set out to raise about $15,000 to make the trip to the US possible, with supporters across the north-west chipping in through raffles and donations.
Then came the call from the Mount Isa Rodeo to the shock and delight of her family.
"Blew me away, made me cry actually," Mr Kennedy said.
"It's got us there. It's got us over the line."
Backing the young ones
The Mount Isa Rodeo has already had to fight for its own future.
The event fell into voluntary administration in September 2024, before a group of residents rallied to revive it for last year, bringing it back before a record crowd.
Now the board is turning its attention to the riders coming through.
Mount Isa Rodeo vice-chair Marcus Curr said developing young riders was becoming an important part of the organisation's future.
"A lot of kids in the bush … don't get to play cricket and football as much as city kids do," he said.
"So rodeo is a big part of their life and their culture."
The board runs an annual junior clinic where young people including children from remote communities learn about safety, technique and competition.
Mr Curr estimated about 50 children attended this year.
Smaller rodeos across the region also give young competitors somewhere to build their skills before stepping into the Kalkadoon Arena.
Mr Curr said the Murphy brothers and Cade Ferguson were examples of what can happen when talent was matched with family support and opportunities to compete.
"If there's talent around, we've got to support them and encourage them and give them opportunities," he said.
Beyond the Kalkadoon Arena
Mr Curr said he wanted the Mount Isa Rodeo to become "more than just running a rodeo for the weekend".
"It's about investing in opportunities for kids and having Mount Isa Rodeo being a part of Australia developing some of the best cowboys and cowgirls in the world," he said.
For Lareece, one of those opportunities is already waiting in the United States, with plenty of pressure and expectation.
But ask what she loves most about bull riding and the answer is much simpler.
"Winning and holding on."

title: The commodification of Indigenous cultures and traditions
content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.
For many Indigenous communities, the traditions, art, and ceremonies are the backbone of their shared identity, essential for marking important milestones, fostering a sense of community, and passing on histories to the younger generation. However, all too often, these traditions are extracted, repackaged, sold, or seized for someone else’s gain.
Spiritual ceremonies get restaged for tourists. Manufacterers co-opt Indigenous art without credit or payment. Governments annex Indigenous heritage to legitimize their own power. The mechanics differ across geography and culture, but the result is the same: Resources and meaning flow outward from the community that created them and enrich outsiders — often the same groups that have been oppressing them for centuries.
In Oaxaca, Mexico, wedding planners sell “Oaxacan weddings” as a commercial package, offering calenda processions, mezcal, and traditional dancing, stripped of the ceremonies and reciprocity that give the tradition its meaning.
Meanwhile, major international fashion houses shamelessly lift Indigenous textile patterns, profiting off their designs while failing to give credit or payment to those who conceived of them. But this story isn’t only about extraction: In Guatemala, Maya weavers are fighting back, pushing for legal recognition of their collective intellectual property rights.
In Southern Mexico, Oaxacan communities have a rich tradition of elaborate wedding ceremonies that are being commodified and monetized to reach outside audiences. Oaxacan weddings typically involve elements like calenda (a traditional Oaxacan procession), Guelaguetza (a traditional Oaxacan festival), as well as specific food, music, dance, drink, and rituals.
These “Oaxacan wedding packages” strip the events of all of their cultural significance and reduce them to a transaction. As Oaxacan author Kupijy Vargas explains:
El concepto de bodas oaxaqueñas está ofertado en un mercado comercial, ofrecido al público por paquetes, construidos a partir de la apropiación cultural de una calenda, incluyendo el mezcal, la música y las mujeres bailando.
Estos paquetes ofrecen ese concepto para después tener una fiesta en el jardín etnobotánico, en donde se sirve comida oaxaqueña gourmet, alimentos que se comen dentro de la región pero servidos de manera estilizada. Quienes los preparan y los sirven, es decir, los meseros, cocineras, etcétera, son quienes sostienen con sus atenciones a esa fiesta en donde no existe la Guelaguetza, ni el acto de dar y recibir, sino que existe una monetización por los servicios. Es allí cuando el colonialismo vuelve a triunfar, convirtiendo en trabajadores a todas esas personas de la cultura en la que crecieron y nacieron, en sus propias tierras.
The concept of Oaxacan weddings is marketed commercially, offered to the public in packages built upon the cultural appropriation of a calenda (a traditional Oaxacan procession), including mezcal, music, and women dancing.
These packages offer this concept followed by a party in the ethnobotanical garden, where gourmet Oaxacan food is served — foods eaten within the region but presented in a stylized manner. Those who prepare and serve the food — the waiters, cooks, and so on — are the ones who sustain this party with their attention to detail. There is no Guelaguetza (a traditional Oaxacan festival), no act of giving and receiving, but rather a monetization of services. It is here that colonialism triumphs once again, turning all those people of the culture in which they grew up and were born, in their own land, into mere laborers.
A similar dynamic unfolds with textiles in this region and other Indigenous communities. Oaxacan author Tajëëw B. Díaz Robles argues that extracting traditional textiles without acknowledging or compensating the communities that invented them is a form of appropriation.
…propongo que el plagio y/o apropiación de la blusa de Tlahui y de sus patrones gráficos por parte de Isabel Marant y Antik Batik (otra empresa de moda francesa que también incurrió en la copia del textil de Tlahui en su colección Bartra de 2014) es la conversión de formas diversas de derechos de propiedad colectiva-comunal a propiedad privada, puesto que hasta el momento del plagio los bordados eran considerados parte de la identidad cultural de un colectivo, un textil cuyos patrones gráficos identifican a una comunidad en específico y que se recrea comunitariamente. Esto no significa que no sean personas específicas las que las elaboran ni que no exista una comercialización local, pero estas personas crean y producen en un contexto comunitario delimitado y las prendas circulan en un mercado que identifica claramente su origen. De ahí que Marant y Antik Batik, en palabras de las autoridades comunitarias de Tlahuitoltepec en su pronunciamiento de junio de 2015, hayan cometido algo que enuncian como ‘la apropiación de un patrimonio cultural.’
I propose that the plagiarism and/or appropriation of the Tlahui blouse and its graphic patterns by Isabel Marant and Antik Batik (a French fashion company that also copied the Tlahui textile in its 2014 Bartra collection) constitutes the conversion of various forms of collective/communal property rights into private property. Until the plagiarism, the embroidery was considered part of a collective’s cultural identity, a textile whose graphic patterns identify a specific community and are recreated communally.
This does not mean that specific individuals do not create them, nor that local commerce does not exist, but these individuals create and produce within a defined community context, and the garments circulate in a market that clearly identifies their origin. Therefore, Marant and Antik Batik, in the words of the Tlahuitoltepec community authorities in their June 2015 statement, committed what they describe as ‘the appropriation of cultural heritage.’
Some Maya communities in Guatemala are fighting back against this phenomenon by pushing for legal protections for traditional crafts and textiles.
The fight has been going on for over a decade: In 2016, the Women’s Association for the Development of Sacatepéquez (AFEDES) and a coalition of weaving cooperatives filed a constitutional challenge arguing that Guatemala’s silence on Indigenous textile rights was itself unconstitutional. The Constitutional Court sided with them twice, ordering Congress to pass protective legislation. Thus far, Congress has failed to do so. Two bills have died in the legislature: Initiative 5247 in 2017, and Initiative 6136 in 2022.
In June 2026, the movement, now working under the name “Ru Chajixik ri Qana'ojb'äl” (“safeguarding our knowledge,” in the Kaqchikel language), delivered a third proposal, Initiative 6788.
Like its predecessors, the bill defines textile intellectual property as “collective, inalienable, and imprescriptible,” meaning it belongs to the community rather than any individual, can’t be sold or signed away, and can’t expire.
If passed, it would formally recognize Indigenous peoples as the legal authors of their weavings, designs, and techniques — including specific motifs, patterns, symbols, colors, glyphs, and petroglyphs passed down through generations — and create a National Council on Textile and Indigenous Clothing Intellectual Property to enforce those rights. The weavers have also asked Congress for three concrete commitments alongside the bill itself: A favorable ruling affirming the constitutional and international legal basis for collective Indigenous intellectual property, expedited legislative handling, and a standing dialogue between Congress and the movement to track the bill’s progress.
Regardless of how the bill fares in Guatemala’s legislature, the proposal presents a model for other Indigenous groups around the world looking to safeguard their own intellectual property rights.

title: The moving lessons of nomadic herders
content:
The moving lessons of nomadic herders
Loading...
The summer of 2026 hasn’t just been a time for pastoral relaxation in the great outdoors; it’s also been a season of, and for, pastoralists. Global events have brought together hundreds of representatives from communities whose lives and livelihoods are built on pastoral or nomadic herding traditions.
On Monday, the sixth World Nomad Games kicked off in Kyrgyzstan, a former Soviet republic in Central Asia. Hundreds of participants are competing in horse races and horseback wrestling, falconry, and archery, among other events.
Meanwhile, over the preceding two weeks, at a conference in Mongolia – where about a third of the population is nomadic – pastoralists from around the world advocated for rights to public grazing lands and freer movement.
The United Nations has designated 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists – a sign of the movement to recognize pastoralists’ roles and rights as contributing citizens and sources of practical expertise and cultural pride. It denotes an evolving humility and respect among governments and scientists who are seeking ways to incorporate the traditional approaches into a modern system long defined by distinct boundaries, increasing urbanization, and regulated resource access.
The Mongolia meeting, Le Monde pointed out last month, marked a shift from viewing nomadic groups and their practices as “a driver of land degradation” to recognizing their “many benefits: maintaining landscapes, preserving biodiversity, preventing fires, adding value to regions and enabling adaptation to climate change.”
The world’s estimated 500 million pastoralists have fine-tuned the skill of living off the meat, dairy, fibers, and hides produced by their herds of sheep, cattle, camels, yaks, reindeer, and llamas. And they’ve done this while regularly on the move – across the Arctic regions of North America and Scandinavia, the steppes of Russia and Central Asia, mountains of South America and South Asia, and the arid reaches of Africa and the Middle East.
As countries have pursued economic growth and industrialization, pastoralism was seen as antiquated and inconvenient– as a system to be “modernized,” sometimes forcibly. Now, the challenges of severe weather and desertification present risks of similar forced responses, including mandatory restrictions on herd sizes and herders’ movements.
But in other quarters, there’s recognition that the potential threats of climate change can be turned into opportunities for community cohesion and repair. In southern India, for example, villagers are allowing – and even paying – herders to use their land in exchange for dung, the natural fertilizer that farmers need to produce higher-value organic crops.
At the conference in Mongolia, nomadic representatives sought ideas as well as funding to help protect their livelihoods. Alongside that, as the environmental news site Mongabay reported, they sought something less tangible – official acknowledgment of what they have to offer through their accumulated knowledge in adapting to changing landscapes.
Such explicit and shared recognition among humankind has inestimable value.

title: New assessment finds five EU Missions are driving systemic change
content:
All five EU Missions are making steady progress towards their objectives – with the Climate Adaptation Mission having already met and surpassed its 2030 targets.
The five EU Missions were launched in 2021 under Horizon Europe 2021-2027. They are designed to translate scientific and technological innovation into practical solutions that can be tested and deployed in real-life settings across Europe, addressing pressing societal challenges – climate change, soil and waters health, and cancer – by going beyond traditional instruments and giving research and innovation a new role. Their time-bound objectives help mobilise coordinated action and support long-term societal transformation.
According to the assessment, all five EU Missions are making good progress towards their 2030 goals:
Climate Adaptation:
The goal of this mission is to support at least 150 European regions, local authorities and communities to become climate resilient. The target has already been largely surpassed, with 292 regional and local authorities having already implemented climate adaptation measures.
Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities:
Its objective is to support at least 100 cities in achieving climate neutrality, and to inspire other cities across Europe. Currently, already 107 cities have Climate City Contracts. They are projected to cut emissions by 76% by 2030, backed by more than €13 billion in supported or developing investment.
Cancer:
Its aim is to improve the lives of more than 3 million people through prevention, early detection, treatment and care for not only those affected by cancer, but also their families. The current actions show that it will be able to improve the lives of 2.3 million people by 2030. Upcoming projects expected to raise this figure beyond the target of 3 million.
Restore our Ocean and Waters:
The goal is to restore the health of our ocean and waters by protecting and restoring aquatic ecosystems, reducing pollution and making the blue economy carbon-neutral and circular. It has delivered 121 innovative solutions tested in 349 real-world demonstration sites, engaged 86 regions in replication efforts and secured over 1,000 Charter Actions from stakeholders. Under the Mission, the design of the core infrastructure of the European Digital Twin Ocean – expected to be fully operational by 2030 – was completed and is now accessible to all.
A Soil Deal for Europe:
The Mission is progressing towards its goal of 100 Living Labs, with 45 already established. It involves over 500 real sites (such as farms) across Europe, and 60 to 70 additional ones are expected to become operational by 2028.
According to a mid-term assessment published by the European Commission, the five EU Missions in Horizon Europe are delivering tangible positive results in addressing some of Europe’s most pressing societal challenges through scientific and technological innovation.

title: Togo's sacred Voodoo stone augers year of peace and prosperity
content:
Togo
A canoe glided slowly across the waters of Lake Togo, carrying the mystical Aklima tam-tam drum to a sacred wood to herald a momentous event: the 363rd unveiling of the sacred stone.
For the Guin people, the annual Epe-Ekpe or Ekpessosso festival in September marks the start of the new ancestral year.
The traditional "taking of the sacred stone" ceremony is an integral rite dating back to 1663 and started by settlers from the former Gold Coast -- modern-day Ghana.
Believers eagerly await the emergence of the stone, whose colour, which varies from year to year, is interpreted as a sign of what the coming 12 months will bring.
"The stone can be several colours: white, a symbol of peace and prosperity; sky blue, a sign of abundant food crops; or red, heralding a year of famine, war and misfortune," said Wlomo Nomo Combietey VIII Nii Labite, guardian of the sacred wood.
But "it can also be multicoloured, a sign of disease or a major epidemic", added the ceremonial guardian.
This year's stone augurs well for the 12 months ahead, being white.
As every year for the past three-and-a-half centuries, several hundred people, the majority Voodoo priests and priestesses, gathered in Glidji-Kpodji Square, near the southern city of Aneho, to witness the emergence of the stone, known as "Ekpessosso."
In Togo, a country of seven million people, 51 percent of the population practises Voodoo, which has multiple forms.
That is more than those who follow Christianity and Islam combined in the small west African nation.
Dressed in white loincloths and adorned with several strings of pearls, followers sing and dance for hours on end, some entering a trance-like state.
Thursday saw a frenzied crowd gather to witness a select group of believers emerge from the wood carrying the oval-shaped stone.
A Voodoo priest then cradled the stone as the crowd chanted "Helu-lo, helu-lo," meaning woe to evil spirits in the Mina language.
"The white stone heralds a year of purity, peace and prosperity," the priest proclaimed from a small podium.
"The gods have answered our prayers," exulted a relieved Pierrette Ahouefa, a priestess clad in multicoloured beads.
"The rituals began in early June in all the convents and the sacred forest. Each step is followed to the letter," said fellow priestess Jeanne Sika.
The nature-based Voodoo belief system emerged in the late 16th century in the town of Tado on the Mono river, which separates Togo from eastern neighbour Benin.
Followers worship a single god, the Mahu or Segbo-Lissa, through more than 200 deities.

title: Hundreds of children embracing te reo swim safety lessons
content:
Kapiti Coast hosts te reo swimming event
A swimming sports event on the Kāpiti Coast has given a few hundred local kids the chance to flex their skills in the water - while speaking entirely in te reo.
Three schools from Ōtaki, Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Te Rito, Te Kura ā iwi o Whakatupuranga Rua Mano and Te Kura o Ōtaki, took part in Kauroa Ahurei in Paraparaumu on Thursday, learning about water safety in a space created specifically for te reo Māori.
Kauora Ahurei organiser Terina Raureti said the idea for the event came from her nieces and nephews, who wanted the chance to use their swimming skills in a competitive setting.
"It's really important to me that they don't have to change who they are to come to Kauora, and that's the whole point that it was created, because we want our kids to be able to fully immerse in their mātauranga, in their worldview, in their reo Māori, to learn how to swim and to engage in the taiao and the wai in a way that is actually reflective of how they live their lives."
The events are based on the pūkenga wai (water competencies) of Kauora, one of those pūkenga is kauawhi, which involves putting on a lifejacket before jumping in the pool.
"It's just knowing that they are in these competitive environments putting on a lifejacket, the stress and just having that moment to think, 'oh yeah, that's how you put it on properly', and we've got to put it on properly before that buzzer goes off.
"So yeah, it's just kind of teaching everyone about the importance of equipment as well, and it's not just about the swimming skills, it's about all the resources around it as well."
Raureti said a lot of the time whānau aren't actually going to the water to swim, they're going to dive or to fish, so it's crucial that kids learn about the equipment too.
There were a lot of inequities in water safety statistics between Māori and non-Māori, and that was reflected in the inequities in access to aquatics and water safety programmes, she said.
"So teaching our kids to love the water, rather than teaching them about all the dangers and all the things. Because we do get stereotyped as a community that we are at high risk... but we're actually a really beautiful water community, and it's just about making sure that our tamariki know that about the water, and where the risks are versus what you can do safely."
Jade Ratapu works at Te Kōhanga Reo o Raukawa but she was also there as a parent, with her son taking part in his first swimming sports event.
"I te hīkaka i te ata nei, oho moata, whakariterite i ōna kākahu. I tae mai ki te puna i kitea i te marea i āhua pā te āmaimai ki ā ia, engari kātahi anō i tutuki pai i tōna reihi."
He was excited this morning, woke up early and got his clothes ready, but when we arrived at the pool and saw all the people he felt a bit nervous, but his race ended well.
Ratapu feels very lucky that her son can attend a swim class every week, also run by Kauora, that is conducted in te reo.
"Ka timata āhua āmaimai ngā tamariki, kāre e pīrangi kia ruku, kia māku ngā karu, engari i te mutunga iho kua kaha kitea ngā painga i tēnei rā, ki ngā tamariki kōhanga o mua kei rō i te puna papaku i te puna hōhonu hoki i tēnei rā, kua kite i te māia."
[The kids at Kōhanga Reo] often start off nervous, they don't want to dive in or get their eyes wet, but we have really seen the benefits today for the kids who used to be in Kōhanga and are now in the shallow pool or even the deep pool, we've really seen the confidence in them.
Nukuao and Hawaiki are just two of the volunteers who help keep the Ahurei running.
"Ki au nei ko te whakahirahiratanga ko tō tātau nei reo Māori me te kite i te pakaritanga ō ngā kura Māori, me ētahi kura Pākehā anō hoki e kaha aro ana ki tō tātau nei reo, waihoki ki ō rātau pakaritanga i roto i te reo," Nukuao said.
To me what is most important about this event is our language, and seeing the strength of the Māori schools, and some of the Pākehā schools who are paying attention to the language, in speaking te reo.
Hawaiki said the event was about whakawhanaungatanga, kotahitanga and friendly competition between the three kura.
"It's cool to teach all the kids Kauora and te reo Māori and to teach them swimming in a Māori way."

title: Brazil protects 1.6 million acres, creates 4 Amazon reserves, and expands Caatinga park
content:
More than 1.6 million acres of Brazilian ecosystems have been placed under protection, expanding conservation efforts in a country considered one of the most ecologically important on Earth.
The newly protected area spans parts of the Amazon and the Caatinga. The measures aim to preserve biodiversity while supporting local communities and Indigenous territories.
Here's what to know
According to an Instagram post from actor and environmental advocate Leonardo DiCaprio, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva announced on September 8 that four Sustainable Development Reserves would be established in the Amazon and that Sete Cidades National Park in the Caatinga would be enlarged.
All four reserves are in the region around the BR-319 highway, and they are meant to safeguard biodiversity while helping defend Indigenous Peoples' ancestral territories.
In Piauí, Sete Cidades National Park is being expanded by more than 17,000 acres (6,900 hectares). DiCaprio said the added protection benefits threatened species, including the endemic Cerrado Little Brown Bat.
Altogether, these new protections total more than 1.6 million acres (676,000 hectares).
More background
This step follows Brazil's establishment of the Rio Tanaru Indigenous Peoples National Park in June 2026.
Protecting intact ecosystems can preserve wildlife habitat, store planet-cooling carbon, and ease pressure from destructive land use.
Sustainable Development Reserves are designed to both conserve nature and to support the people who live in and depend on these landscapes. That can help traditional and local communities maintain livelihoods tied to standing forests, rather than seeing those areas cleared or degraded.
Healthier forests help regulate rainfall, stabilize regional climates, and protect freshwater systems that millions of people rely on directly or indirectly. Stronger protection for Indigenous territories also aligns with long-standing evidence that Indigenous stewardship is among the most effective forms of conservation.
What's being done?
The designations also come with major funding commitments. DiCaprio said more than $47 million is tied to sustainable forest management, along with more than $46 million for restoration and territorial initiatives.
The money is expected to help pay for territorial protection, restoration work, community-led projects, and forest management.
DiCaprio also said the designations received support from @andesamazonfund, Re:wild, @artintoacres, @bezosearthfund, @moorefound, and the Wyss Foundation.
He wrote that these are "important efforts to protect critical ecosystems while supporting the communities who live in and depend on them."
Where can I learn more?
Brazil's new reserves are part of an effort to slow deforestation, repair damaged landscapes, and rebuild the country's environmental vigor. The stories below look at how policy shifts, better monitoring, and reforestation work are affecting the Amazon and other ecosystems across Brazil.
• Across the Amazon, surging deforestation spurred the Brazilian government into stronger conservation action.
• Brazil's native seed networks face obstacles even as its 30-million-acre reforestation plan moves forward.
• In Brazil, improved monitoring helped the Atlantic Forest reach its lowest deforestation in 40 years.
Protected areas tend to have the biggest impact when enforcement, restoration, and tangible political support back them.

title: Back-to-school rituals that help these families calm first-day jitters
content:
This week, Libby Barnicke and her family will engage in what has become, for them, an important tradition. She’ll dress up her two boys in their crisp new school uniforms and line them up on the front porch for their annual back-to-school photo.
It’s a tradition that is replicated in households from coast to coast. For many families, these early weeks of September are a major occasion. The end of summer, and the start of a new year.
“I always view September as the new year. Not January first,” said Ms. Barnicke, who lives in Toronto. “It feels like the beginning. Like a renewal. It’s excitement, but also a lot of anxiousness.”
It’s a month that brings new milestones in many families. The start of a new routine, or adventure, or challenge. A new step toward independence. For many, it will be their first day in a new place.
The Globe and Mail spoke with four families experiencing “first days” this week. Here’s what they told us about how they feel, and how they’re preparing:
First day of kindergarten: Aadhya Trivedi, 4 years old
Aadhya is a chatty preschooler who lives in Toronto with her family. She knows how to spell her own name, and how to count to four fingers when asked her age. She likes rainbow-coloured tutus, chapatis with curried vegetables and reading books with her mom. When she grows up, she plans on being a doctor and also a princess.
What she’s most excited about
Aadhya’s older brother already attends the school where she’s headed, so he’s given her some ideas on what to expect.
“Kindergarten,” she said, “is where you help your teachers. Cleaning. Putting books away. Sitting in the circle.”
She’s most excited to see the school library, which her brother has described in great detail. She can’t wait to pick out her own books and bring them home.
What she’s worried about
Aadhya will miss the comforts of daycare. “The teachers love me a lot. I love my teachers a lot.”
She’ll miss her daycare friends, too. “I love my friends,” she said. “We hug with each other and hold each other’s hands.”
She’ll be parting ways with almost all of them. Most are heading off to a different school, so she’ll have to make new friends. When asked if this makes her nervous, she gives the tiniest nod.
“The new friends might hate me, and might not love me,” she said. “They might not want to be best friends with me.”
How the family is preparing
“She’s already been in the daycare setting, so the routine is kind of the same,” said her mom, Sonali. They’ve been working as a family to drill the importance of that morning routine in to their children: Of waking up by a specific time and leaving plenty of room each morning to get ready and out the door without feeling rushed.
Beyond that, Sonali said she’s been focused on preparing Aadhya for the practical challenges of kindergarten such as how to get through a full day without an afternoon nap, how to recognize her own name at her cubby and how to tell the difference between her stuff and all the other kids’, which often look similar.
Aadhya is also practicing how to open and close her own lunch bag and food containers. It’ll be her first time bringing lunch from home, and she’ll have to figure out how to navigate that. “It’s all about keeping things simple and accessible,” said Sonali.
First day rituals
Each year, Sonali asks family and friends to send in short video messages for the kids with their well-wishes for the new school year. She compiles all of them into a larger video that the family watches the night before school. They make popcorn, settle into the couch and make a night of it.
“It’s a tradition that we all look forward to,” Sonali said.
The transition from summer to a new school year is always an anxious, nerve-wracking time. “And, honestly not just for the kids,” she said.
“It’s emotional for the parents too – seeing your babies going out into the world.”
First day of middle school: Taylor, 12
Until recently, Taylor attended a co-ed, public Catholic school in Toronto, where he lives with his family. But this week he is moving to an all-boys, private middle school that is connected to a high school. So he’ll be sharing the halls for the first time with kids who are much older, ranging from Grade 7 all the way up to Grade 12.
What he’s most excited about
Taylor is an athlete who plays soccer, football and hockey. “Any sport, basically.” So he’s looking forward to the new sports and activities available.
“It’s a lot bigger than my [former] school, so there’s lots of different types of activities and clubs,” he said. “It’s just a totally different environment.”
He’s also looking forward to the fact that he’ll be joined by many of his existing friends who are moving to the new school alongside him.
What he’s most worried about
“Probably the exams.” The curriculum in middle school, he expects, will be much more intense.
How they’re preparing
This week will represent a big step into independence for Taylor, said his mom Libby. Instead of getting dropped off and picked up by his parents each day, he’ll be responsible for getting himself to and from school.
For the first time, Taylor will have to navigate public transit on his own. He’ll also have to figure out where to buy his snacks after school, and how to pay for them. The family is having to discuss, for the first time, questions such as whether he’s ready for a debit card or a cellphone.
“It’s a change in tide,” said Libby. “We’re having meaningful conversations about what the new routine is going to look like – early adult conversations, I would say.”
Back to school rituals
This will be the seventh year that Libby has lined up her boys for their back-to-school photo (they missed one year because of the pandemic). “It’s just always been a marker for me to show the progress – to show just how big they’re getting.”
Still, beyond the anxiety and the nerves, she said, there’s a lot of excitement.
“I think there’s something very joyful about coming of age, and moving on,” she said. “I just can’t wait to see what he does with this next chapter.”
First day of high school: Arshia Purohit Singh, 13
At first glance, Arshia seems like a typical Vancouver teenager. She likes sushi and swimming, music by Olivia Rodrigo and Sabrina Carpenter and books from the popular ‘Powerless’ YA series by Lauren Roberts.
But, if you spend just a minute talking to her, it’s clear that she’s no ordinary kid. Arshia was the valedictorian at her elementary school and runs her own small business online. She organizes fundraisers for the local children’s hospital and intends to be a lawyer one day – after graduating from Harvard Law School, of course.
She’s made the difficult decision to attend a different high school (which, in her Vancouver school district, is grades eight through 12) than all of her friends. She’s opting instead for a school with an International Baccalaureate program, which she considers more academically challenging.
What she’s most excited about
Arshia is looking forward to the idea of a challenge. Of more intense classes, and the chance to join the basketball team, the debate club and the students’ council.
“I’m definitely feeling a little bit nervous, but I’m also just really excited for all the new opportunities and all the new people I’m going to meet.”
She’s excited, too, about having a bit more freedom.
“In elementary school, it’s a lot more structured. We were kind of taken to every class, things like that. But in high school, they’ll tell us to go to our different classes, and then it’s just entirely up to us.”
How the family is preparing
The family is big on organization and building good habits. Ever since they were little, Arshia’s mom Sophia Purohit Singh has taught her two kids how to balance their own schedules and make sure they’re staying on top of deadlines.
“The habits were developed way early on, where it was always about keeping yourself busy and organized. Having your own calendar and managing it,” said Sophia. “So there’s not time left over to go on their phone for hours.”
They’ve doubled down on this routine over the summer. Entirely of her own accord, Arshia has been working ahead on her math workbooks (“just to be ready for next year”), and has been talking through with her parents how she might juggle her many new assignments and responsibilities in high school.
Back-to-school rituals
Every year, the family spends at least one day combing through the house to see what school supplies they’ve left lying around.
“It’s stuff we’ve collected over the year, and figuring out how to reuse them,” said Arshia. And then they’ll go back-to-school shopping for everything else.
Back-to-school outfits, said Arshia, “are definitely still a thing.” For her first day of high school, she chose her outfit in advance: A new skirt she bought recently, with a t-shirt and hoodie, in case of cold. “I’m just going to wear what makes me comfortable,” she said.
She knows this is an important moment for her.
“This is kind of a big point of change in my life,” she said. “In a few years, my life is going to change a lot.”
First day of teaching: Nick Erickson, 41
Over the past few decades, Mr. Erickson has been a sawmill worker, a concrete labourer and a logging truck driver. But this week, the father of five from Lake Babine Nation in B.C. will take on a new career: A high-school teacher.
He’s a new graduate of NITEP, the Indigenous Teacher Education Program at the University of British Columbia, where, after going back to school in his late 30s, he recently graduated with a bachelor’s degree in education. He’ll be teaching a small group of Indigenous students, grades eight through 12, at a high school in his community.
“My goal is to give Indigenous students the confidence to go on to bigger and better things. To show them they’re capable,” he said.
“If I can do it at the age of 41, there’s no reason why anybody else can’t do it.”
What he’s excited about
Mr. Erickson can only recall ever having one Indigenous teacher when he was growing up. “It was the only classroom where I felt like I wasn’t really being judged,” he said. Now, he’s excited to be that positive role model for his own students.
“I have a lot of life stories. I’ve had a lot of things happen in my life that I can relate with the kids.”
Plus, as the father of five daughters (who range in age from eight to 25), he has ample confidence and experience in dealing with teenagers.
As a teacher, he said, he won’t be “Mr. Erickson.” Just “Nick.”
“I want to help them and teach them,” he said. “But I also want to learn beside them.”
One more bonus? His wife, Marsha Erickson, completed the NITEP program alongside him. They’ll be sharing this experience as first-time teachers in the community together.
What he’s worried about
“I’m kind of nervous. I’m responsible for these kids. But if I’m my genuine, authentic self, I’m not going to have any problems. I’m just going to be the best person I can in front of them.”
Back-to-school rituals
Each year, the couple has taken back-to-school pictures of their five kids on the deck in front of the house. This year they’ll take photos again – only this time, with the addition of mom and dad.
